title: Solomonoff induction with reflective oracles
raw_summary: Linkpost for https://arxiv.org/html/2611.14454v1 Our PIBBSS fellow Damini Kusum wrote an excellent paper on prediction with reflective oracle Solomonoff Induction (rOSI). Reflective oracles are best known for their game-theoretic applications, where they are often dismissed because "why would all players choose the same reflective oracle?" It turns out that reflective oracles can also be used to construct a version of Solomonoff induction (called rOSI) with very nice sequence prediction properties - roughly speaking, it can learn to extract computable structure from (partly) uncomputable sequences. In fact, its properties are quite reminiscent of logical induction, but this paper is much shorter and more accessible. In this context, there is only one "player" to choose an oracle, which is just a fixed-point (though you can sort of consider the set of hypotheses entertained by that player as subplayers who share the oracle). I think this paper is the clearest exposition of a very neat but previously obscure idea in agent foundations: self-reflection can overcome unrealizability. Discuss

title: Looping a transformer increases no-CoT capabilities more than general capabilities
raw_summary: Some researchers worry that looping (as in looped transformers ) is a particularly scary way to make AI models more capable, because looped models will be harder to monitor than standard transformers of similar capability. We test this worry on NVIDIA’s Dory 4B, a publicly available looped transformer, and find evidence that it is justified. Result 1. Looping boosts no-CoT reasoning much more than it boosts general capabilities . Dory can run with a configurable number of loops. It was trained to use up to 4 loops, and adding loops up to 8 at inference time still improves performance. Without looping, Dory’s no-CoT capabilities (measured by NCRI, the No-CoT Reasoning Index) match what a trend fitted to open-source models predicts from how well it predicts text (measured in bits-per-byte). Its general with-CoT reasoning capability (measured by “mini-ECI”, a custom, smaller version of Epoch’s Capabilities Index) is high relative to its NCRI, so Dory sits below the NCRI-vs-mini-ECI trend, but it is similar to the best models of its size. Adding loops improves mini-ECI and bits per byte only slightly but increases NCRI substantially. In fact, if we plot NCRI against total parameters, counting looped parameters once per loop, NCRI rises faster than the trend up to 6 loops. This is concerning, since it suggests adding loops increases no-CoT capabilities much more than general capabilities, resulting in models that will be more difficult to monitor. Result 2. Dory has near-zero CoT controllability (ability to follow instructions about what its CoT says or how it is formatted) at every loop count we ran, so we learn little about how looping affects controllability. Remark: Looped transformers can be easily modified to become fully recurrent, as discussed here . We call Dory modified in this way recurrent-Dory, and unmodified Dory normal-Dory. When running Dory with multiple loops (here 2), the middle layers are applied multiple times to the residual stream (left). During ordinary inference, each loop's attention refers to the KV-activations of the corresponding loop in previous token positions (middle). When run with recurrent KV sharing , only the KV activations of the final loop are retained and shared between each loop in subsequent forward passes. The resulting unbounded-depth recurrent computation pathway is marked in orange. Result 3. When we train against CoT monitors, recurrent-Dory learns to obfuscate its reasoning more quickly and completely than normal-Dory. Specifically, after some training, recurrent-Dory can solve serially deep math problems with a rigid structure using only meaningless filler tokens such as ‘ well’ (i.e., we replicated this experiment ). When we RL against a monitor on NCRI tasks, recurrent-Dory generally solves them using a higher fraction of filler tokens than normal-Dory. Result 4. Recurrent-Dory gets significant NCRI uplift with only two loops. Even without any training in this mode, running Dory as a recurrent model can lead to unexpected capability jumps: While increasing the number of loops leads to increasing gains in NCRI in normal mode, for recurrent-Dory, nearly all of the gains are already present at two loops. Implications. GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon all had quite noticeably higher NCRI than the NCRI vs mini-ECI trend would predict, much more above trend than any other model. These models are rumored to be looped transformers. It’s fairly widely accepted that models that can perform more cognition without verbalizing CoT (i.e., no-CoT capabilities) are harder to monitor . Our Result 1 strengthens the empirical case that looping moves a given model steeply upwards in an NCRI-vs-ECI (here mini-ECI) plot, and hence is a particularly scary way to increase capabilities. Looped transformers can also easily be made fully recurrent, and these recurrent models quickly learn to evade monitors under training pressure, which further strengthens the case for concern. Overall, we think our results on Dory make a reasonably strong case that looped transformers are a relatively scary way to increase capabilities. In the rest of the post we’ll present these results in more detail. Result 1: Looping boosts no-CoT reasoning much more than general capabilities In this section, we measure how much looping boosts Dory's no-CoT reasoning and compare it with what trends for standard transformers predict. We hypothesized that Dory would have above-trend no-CoT capabilities. We measure No-CoT capabilities with Neel Nanda's NCRI (No-CoT reasoning index), a suite of math problems of adjustable difficulty. To measure overall capabilities, we use two metrics: Compression factor in terms of bits per byte (bpb) on text collections — this measures pretraining quality and is particularly relevant for base models. Posttraining degrades this a bit. Up to a fixed constant, bpb for a given model is just average pretraining loss multiplied by the tokens per byte ratio (which depends only on the tokenizer and the text corpus). Mini-ECI as a measure of problem solving capabilities for post-trained models. This is a reduced version of ECI computed from a fixed subset of 27 benchmarks in Epoch’s ECI. We keep each benchmark’s difficulty and slope (the per-benchmark parameters of Epoch’s item-response model) fixed at the values determined by Epoch, and estimate each model’s capability from whichever of the 27 benchmarks it has scores on. For most models on the graph, we use scores reported by Epoch; for these mini-ECI differs from ECI by 0.7 points on average (94% within 2 points), with no systematic offset. For Dory and some other models we calculate benchmark scores ourselves. Our runs may differ from Epoch’s because of evaluation settings such as the maximum answer length and sampling parameters. However, Epoch’s own data already mixes runs with different providers and settings, so similar variation is likely present among the comparison models. Result 1.1: Looping increases NCRI much more than pretrain quality; Looped-Dory’s NCRI is well above what the pretraining quality trend would predict. With some exceptions, the relation between compression and NCRI is linear in the tested regime. On unseen text (UncheatableEval) Dory is right on trend when run with 1-loop (i.e. no looping). Increasing the number of loops boosts NCRI substantially (by about 18 points at 8 loops with the best prompt format, and about 13 points with the plain prompt) up to 8 loops, but changes bpb only slightly from one to two loops and not at all after that. The left graph shows bpb for UncheatableEval, which collects recently published text that the models being tested have likely not seen before. The right graph shows bpb on open-source pretraining corpora (on which models may have been trained on). We see that points shift around a bit, but the overall picture doesn’t change very much. Result 1.2. Looping raises NCRI much more than it raises mini-ECI. Plotted against mini-ECI, unlooped Dory has one of the lowest NCRIs relative to trend of any model in the figure. Looping moves Dory sharply up: NCRI rises by about 18 points, while mini-ECI changes by at most about 1.5 points which the trend line says should add only about 2 NCRI points. While looping does raise NCRI much more than it raises mini-ECI, it doesn’t raise it above the mini-ECI vs NCRI trend, even with eight loops. One possible explanation for this is that Dory has strong post-training, leading to unusually high mini-ECI for its no-CoT ability (possibly due to being distilled, or a more recent model). Overall, the fact that it’s still below trend is some evidence against the main point in our post. However, we’d predict that (1) adding more loops would continue to push up NCRI more than mini-ECI, eventually leading it to be substantially above the trendline, and (2) other looped transformers will generally be above trend (e.g., Astra and Argon are well above the trend line, and these are rumored to b…

title: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
raw_summary: I used to think of "automating alignment" as a natural category. But when I tried to think through the strategic implications, I realised that it depends a lot on the type of work. I'm now thinking of it in three buckets: Empirical alignment research : design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for) Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it) Direct alignment work : making particular AI systems more aligned (including via inputs such as training data) In the rest of this post I'll walk through my current takes on these in terms what’s needed for automation, how good or bad they look, what our priorities might be (to the extent we're interested in automating alignment [1] ), etc. Automating empirical alignment research This is the most obvious fit for the AI capabilities we’re getting at the moment. You want to know more about the relationship between some alignment-relevant variables? Great, an AI agent can design and run that experiment for you. You want to know what training methods help your alignment benchmark go up? In the not-too-distant future, AI agents will probably be able to do this too. When we have the automated capabilities researchers we seem on track for, this is exactly the kind of thing they’ll likely be able to do a lot of. Note that I’m not counting the design of benchmarks/metrics/evals as part of this bucket. In current practice that’s tightly intertwined with empirical alignment research, and often the hardest part of it. But for automation purposes it clusters much more with conceptual work; it’s easy to imagine automating the rest of empirical research without it (as AI capabilities generally get automated); and I think its automation has different strategic upshots. The capabilities that are needed for automating empirical alignment research very heavily overlap with the capabilities needed for automating AI capabilities research. Therefore, it doesn’t seem like a priority to try to accelerate this type of automation. However, the prospect of getting a lot of automated empirical alignment work before we have good versions of other types of automated alignment work increases the priority of work which complements it. Significantly, that may mean better specification of the kind of numbers we would like measured/targeted. Automating conceptual alignment research What about automating the type of metric choice/construction that we’ve just said would be a good complement to automating empirical alignment work? Or more generally improving our understanding of how to think about alignment, what we’re even aiming for, etc.? This is essentially theoretical research. Automating it is trickier than automating empirical work because of the lack of verifiable signal about what constitutes progress. Accelerating the automation of conceptual research is somewhat fraught (feeding into some dangerous technologies), but seems helpful for a number of high-priority areas, including macrostrategy as well as conceptual alignment work. Overall it seems likely good to do, if we can. Methods for helping to automate conceptual research broadly might include: Curating training data for finetuning Building scaffolds to try to elicit more research progress from current or future models Building methods to extract more signal from existing conceptual research data Building benchmarks for conceptual research capabilities, that can be targeted by AI researchers (or potentially by automated capabilities researchers) Or just identifying good ideas for benchmarks, even if they aren’t fully implemented Automating direct alignment work As well as learning more about what it takes to make systems more aligned , sometimes we want to just make our actual systems as aligned as possible . This overlaps with empirical alignment work, but the emphasis is different: Empirical alignment work is science Direct alignment work is engineering Automating direct alignment work could include a lot of activities which leverage scalable cognition for alignment-relevant purposes. This could include careful auditing of particular RL environments or training data, or direct monitoring/supervision of systems during training. RLAIF for alignment properties is a form of automated direct alignment work; Claude 3 Opus’s apparent self-alignment was another (albeit accidental in that case; but if we knew how to reproduce or generalize the behaviour perhaps it could happen deliberately). I think that the limit of automating direct alignment work would be a form of system 2 learning , where updates are not made blindly towards a training objective, but reflectively by an AI system that was already sufficiently aligned (not necessarily having robustly good values already — just enough genuine care about being aligned, and honesty with itself, that its reflective updates tend to move it further in that direction), and wished to become more so — whatever the deep true version of aligned should mean [2] . Embarking on such a path could be fraught (because of difficulty in being confident that the starting conditions were in the right basin of attraction), but compared to other alignment approaches, it has the benefit that it might leverage the full strength of the AI’s cognition to help, so that its “self-improvement” in an alignment direction is a closer analogue to meditation than to self-performed neurosurgery. So, accelerating the automation of direct alignment work could include: Designing (and analysing) setups that can deploy AI labour to help with direct alignment work Designing paradigms (that could then be tested empirically) that allow AI to be a more active participant in its own alignment Producing data (or scaffolds) to help improve AI taste at the alignment-relevant tasks necessary for this Interactions These categories blur and interact in a number of different ways: Automated direct alignment techniques may be good subjects for empirical experiments This is not completely reliant on having good metrics for alignment; developing a science of what’s going on with different attempts at automated direct alignment could be useful even if we don’t yet know what “good” looks like Automated hill-climbing might get you to very strong direct alignment approaches — but this does rely on having good enough metrics i.e. we could plausibly be in a regime where we’re better at reasoning about and implementing training setups that in fact lead to aligned systems than we are at accurately measuring their alignment. In that case, optimising for our best alignment metrics might produce worse alignment outcomes than following our best-guess direct alignment process. If you can do a good job of automating conceptual alignment research, you should be approximately done (“winning” on the alignment challenge) Since that should then be able to do the relevant parts of prep for automating the other types of alignment work, and being appropriately confident in your techniques for them You could also in principle do a good enough job at direct alignment that the systems you’re building are entirely safe But I think it will be hard to have very strong confidence in that before improving our automation of the conceptual side; and so each new generation of AI might pose a challenge — will your alignment techniques transfer, or will your luck run out? So: the main goal (from an existential risk perspective) for automating empirical research and direct alignment work is to get our systems safe enough to robustly avoid catastrophe (“not losing”) for long enough that we can automate conceptual alignment research to a very high quality level There will likely be approaches that allow you to leverage automation of empirical research to get better automation of conceptual work e.g. Taking Talkie or another LLM with only vintage tra…

title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
raw_summary: This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's. This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period. You can adjust various axes of this proposal: Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition. What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints. When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed. One concrete target that I like is: “No checkpoint may be used internally for purposes beyond safety testing, until at least X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor.” This is one specific implementation of internal deployment lags, an idea that the AI Futures Project (AIFP) briefly discusses in How to pace the US frontier as “AI R&D can only be conducted or assisted by AIs that were trained at least 9 months ago”. What does this look like when implemented? Let’s run through a scenario to pin down the details of this proposal. The places where it could go wrong are in the open questions at the end. A legislative body sets a minimum waiting period of X calendar days (starting at 10 and possibly ratcheting up to 90). No checkpoint in a covered model family may be used internally, beyond safety testing, until X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor. Continuing to train a checkpoint’s own weights does not count as internal use. The alternative is for the wait to also block the training of checkpoint N+1, and not just the internal use of checkpoint N. I didn’t go with this because it incentivizes developers to pull out fewer checkpoints for testing, and because delaying training results in an algorithmic overhang. More capable models start exhibiting problems that are harder to surface in short periods (e.g. swarms, long-horizon, memory), so X should possibly increase over time. A model family becomes covered as soon as any of its checkpoints (pre-, mid- or post-trained) is substantially more capable than the last model to complete its wait. If the developer initially claims that the model is not covered but later finds that it is, they will be subject to some penalty (to be determined). There is also an absolute floor on capabilities, so that this doesn’t apply to lots of benign models. In an emergency, the auditor can authorize one named checkpoint to be used early, only for responding to a specific incident (e.g. a harmful model is already causing damage, and the developer has just trained a patched model that could counter it). The standards/legislative body confirms or revokes this within [X days]. The developer continually pulls checkpoints throughout the training process. They first send an auditor a hash, a short fingerprint of the exact weights; then, they carry out safety testing for X days before deploying a checkpoint broadly internally without the below rules. All work has to be fully transparent to auditors. Options for how the X days are structured: Staged testing Stage 1, first part of X: pre-registered evals and named testers in an isolated environment. Stage 2, second part of X: broad monitored internal use, but the model can’t launch jobs, merge code, write to training data, or touch prod. Parallel, hidden runs: whenever someone at the developer uses a cleared model, the new checkpoint gets the same task in a separate sandboxed copy of the environment. Its outputs go only to monitors and the safety team, never back to the person who asked. Open questions The rule itself Should we also allow capability testing? What about ML R&D tasks? One way to game this is to register thousands of tasks from your open R&D backlog, and call running them a capability eval. The outputs are real research (e.g. a faster kernel), and even if you ban using them, people still have to read the transcripts to grade them, so they learn what worked. Pre-registering evals doesn’t help, since it fixes the task list in advance but doesn’t check whether the tasks are live problems. You might end up needing a compute cap. Should we give exemptions for doing safety research? This is an important crux to ask alignment researchers about. Without an exemption, safety research is done with a model that is X days behind, but a blanket exemption lets capabilities work pose as safety work. Should a safety fix (e.g. more post-training, or redoing RL from an earlier checkpoint) restart the X-day wait? It would be bad if it did, as Avi Brach-Neufeld points out here . A developer that finds an issue on day 8 of testing loses more time than one that finds it on day 2, so the rule penalizes finding and fixing problems during the wait. This is probably tolerable at small X, but gets worse as X increases. If safety fixes don’t restart the clock, however, developers could just call capabilities training “safety”. What is the principle behind how much X increases? How large is the risk that an emergency clause would be abused? Concerning behaviours aren’t necessarily caught during pre-deployment testing windows, and are often caught through subsequent monitored internal use. How much are we willing to trade off the value of catching some misaligned behaviours via monitoring internal deployments, vs. being able to pace internal R&D? Which models are covered How is “substantially more capable” defined: effective compute, or something like the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI)? How would an auditor check that the developer has faithfully stuck to the “more capable” definition? How do you avoid bringing classifiers built using a frontier model into scope? Can a developer keep using earlier checkpoints from a family after it becomes covered? A developer could train a second model family and keep it just under the “substantially more capable” line, so it’s never covered. Researchers could then use that family right away, while use of the main family is on hold. This only gets them so far, since coverage is measured against the last model to complete its wait, and an uncovered family never completes one, so the second family can only be ahead by the “substantially more capable” margin. This becomes a bigger problem if the capability measure itself can be gamed. Gaming the wait How can we stop a developer from using a checkpoint for acceleratory AI R&D work during the wait, by labeling that work as an allowed activity (i.e. any AI R&D task whose output gets used for anything other than testing that checkpoint)? How can we cleanly separate out safety testing from other activities? A developer could give a new model a real task during training, such as writing faster training code, and then use that code to train other models before the new model has completed the X-day wait. A developer could make every researcher an A/B tester, so that they use the new model for normal work and rate its answers, and the developer calls this training. Similarly, a developer could have an RL environment that is just how well the model does actual work inside the company. In stage 1 of staged testing, you run the risk that named testers run large agent swarms for capabilities work, in which case the only difference is that there are fewer humans in the loop. This is probably somewhat mitigated by pre-registering evals, but it’s difficult to still allow AWT. In stage 2, you can still copy paste model outputs into training data, or into code and research plans. A developer could also store outputs from the wait and use them the day the checkpoint clears, without breaking any rule. Should there be a blanket ban on training on outputs from the wait, and how would anyone check? In stage 2, how will you detect if the model is launching jobs, merging code, writing to training data, or touching prod? Developers can game the wait by making lots of models and testing all of them at once, s…

title: Q3.5 Timelines Update: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All
raw_summary: We want to get this post out quickly given the urgency of the topic. It’s possible that there are some errors in the modeling, but we think it’s very unlikely that they undermine the high level conclusions. We would love to be corrected on any mistakes we made. METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario . This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) [1] before 2029 . SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs. [2] Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). [3] We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report. [4] . If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement . Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights ( more ). [5] Timelines/Takeoff Update Summary We estimate that METR’s report implies a 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in the pace of progress today, relative to historical levels. This surprises our model; we made our most recent timelines forecasts less than three months ago, and even the most aggressive model-based distribution (Daniel’s) assigned less than 4% to the pace of progress being sped up by at least 1.7x in November 2026. [6] 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration is a bigger deal than it may seem; e.g., it’s a much bigger deal than making employees 1.7x more productive . We focus in this post primarily on forecasting when Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will arrive. We also discuss Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI): AIs that are better than top human experts at virtually all tasks. ( more ) In this post, we forecast SAR and TED-AI using the following approaches: Simple models: Research taste linear extrapolation : Even assuming that the recent pace of progress doesn’t accelerate further due to automation, the fact that the recent trend is above historical rates is a big update to our timelines; a linear extrapolation of the recent rate of AI progress predicts that SAR will likely be achieved by the end of 2027. Labor uplift extrapolation : An exponential extrapolation of self-reported labor uplift predicts SAR in mid-2028. In addition to not modeling automation, there are reasons to think that an exponential is too conservative. However, self-reports may be too bullish. Extrapolating Anthropic automation levels : Anthropic recently shared a graph showing how the percentage of R&D tasks at various automation levels has changed over time. Extrapolating this predicts SAR in late 2027; this method also doesn’t model speedup from automation. Extrapolating software R&D uplift per unit of ECI : AI software R&D uplift must have recently been increasing by a larger factor with each ECI point. If we linearly extrapolate the rate at which this “factor of extra uplift per ECI point” is increasing, we get SAR in Dec 2027 (if we assume that the self-reported AI labor uplift chart is accurate) or July 2027 (if we assume that there was no meaningful automation 12 months ago and all the speed-up has happened after then). Tom Davidson’s toy model: Predicts superintelligence in around a year conditional on a software-only singularity, so SAR sometime in 2027. Filtered AI Futures Model (AIFM) : Keeping the existing AIFM (including parameter distributions), and filtering for trajectories that match METR’s AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration estimates. This serves 2 purposes on top of the simple extrapolations: Modeling how automation changes the rate of progress, allowing forecasting reasonably beyond SAR. Informing what parameter settings in the simple research taste extrapolation are plausible. The results of these methods: How to think about these results: The simple research taste extrapolation, which is a simplified version of the AIFM, gives July or September 2027, depending on whether you account for parameter uncertainty. Other simple models predict late 2027 to mid-2028. When conditioned on 1.7x Nov 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, the AIFM predicts a SAR median of Feb 2027. This is faster than the simple research taste extrapolation because it usually has a higher level of Sep 2026 research taste (in the median case, matching a median researcher), [7] and it accounts for further automation. When additionally conditioning on a 1.2x May 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, predictions get slower because it indicates a lower rate of growth than is typical when only conditioning on 1.7x in Nov. We then explore hypotheses for why the AI Futures Model was wrong , including parameter adjustments and modeling changes. The analysis is highly preliminary, and we were unable to come to strong conclusions. Our top candidates for what explains where we went wrong are: Near-AC coding skills result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated . This could explain the combination of ~1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in Nov and (very roughly) ~1.2x in May, without AIs already having high enough research taste to contribute to the acceleration. In this case, the gradual acceleration no longer implies a low research taste slope, so steeper slopes and faster taste-driven takeoffs are more likely. Skills besides coding and research taste (the two included in the AIFM), e.g., data generation, are driving acceleration. This potentially would have similar implications to the above bullet. But it’s unclear. Conversion of uplift to pace of progress is too conservative. I.e., we modeled diminishing returns to AI research effort too harshly. This would point toward a faster takeoff. Here’s an example trajectory from the AIFM showing how things might go if the cause of our prediction error was underestimating AI R&D uplift from near-AC coding skills: [8] After discussing some other considerations , we share our all-things-considered forecasts (conditional on AGI projects/companies not slowing down): Note that the gap between a person’s SAR median and TED-AI median is not their median time from SAR to TED-AI. Because the distributions of the time until SAR and of the time from SAR to TED-AI both have long right tails, the difference of the medians is typically larger than the median of the difference, so subtracting the two columns tends to overstate the median time between the two milestones. METR’s estimates imply that progress is currently sped up by 1.7x due to AI In METR’s recent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic , they estimate that, over the past year, AI R&D progress has accelerated by ~2x relative to the trend before Oct 2025. METR estimates that ~80% of current acceleration is downstream of AI (as opposed to other factors), which implies a 1.7x acceleration due to AI (1.67–1.74x depending on how the 80% is read; see appendix ). title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
raw_summary: (Thanks to @Goutham Nalagatla for discussion and for sitting with me and talking about it while I wrote it.) METR recently released a report estimating that Anthropic is getting an overall 1.7x acceleration in AI capability progress as a result of AI accelerating their work. As many have noted (see e.g. Ajeya’s post ), this 1.7x acceleration implies that research is being sped up by much more than 1.7x; Ajeya speculates 10x (which is similar to the ~12x uplift estimated by Anthropic staff). That is, this result implies that researchers are producing about 10 times as many quality-adjusted results as they would without AI progress, or as they were a year or two ago. Anthropic researchers estimated that Mythos 5 caused 5x uplift, and we have access to Opus 5.5, which is somewhat better. (I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising (see Ryan’s discussion at the time), but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report). If this is the case, then AIs speed up AI safety research as much as AI capabilities research, we might expect Anthropic safety researchers to be working 10x faster, and external safety researchers to be working 5x faster now and 10x faster soon. And external safety researchers can probably scale compute use faster than Anthropic capabilities researchers can . For example, we at Redwood are well-funded and would totally 5x our compute spend if we had 5x as many experiments to run, unlike Anthropic capabilities researchers who are presumably already doing a pretty good job of using all the compute they have. So I think that we should expect a 5x labor acceleration to turn into more like a 5x research project acceleration. I don't think our empirical research has been going 5x faster since we got access to Fable/Opus 5.5; I would have guessed more like 2-3x speedup. Why is this? Maybe we suck and have not adopted AI as effectively as Anthropic capabilities researchers have. This might be the case. Obviously, Redwood researchers extensively use AI agents for their research, mostly using Claude Code and recently Claude Tag. We also have an in-house scaffold for autonomous AI research, which has produced results that we've published in the past (e.g. here , here ), though we haven't put a lot of work into using or improving this scaffold in the last few months. We found that this research scaffold is pretty good at doing empirical research, but Claude sometimes makes extremely unhinged choices that invalidate its results and is also pretty bad at writing up its findings; these weaknesses substantially reduced how quickly we could use it to produce useful research outputs. If Anthropic had scaffolds that made their models drastically more useful, I expect they would have turned them into products? Maybe they get a lot of uplift from Anthropic-specific infra for their AIs? Maybe they don’t release scaffold features that are specifically useful for ML research? Overall, I think this is maybe a partial explanation, but it seems sort of surprising for our uplift to be way smaller than Anthropic’s. It’s really felt like fundamental weaknesses of the models, rather than scaffold limitations, are the main reason that they haven’t been more useful to us. To some extent, our work is probably less accelerated by AI than Anthropic capabilities research is. I think most of our empirical research is similarly well-suited to AI speedup to most published ML capabilities research. Maybe Anthropic capabilities research is particularly well suited to AI speedup compared to most ML research? Some of the pretraining work may rely more on the AI's strengths. This could be the case if, for example, a big blocker on running experiments on new architectures is implementing them efficiently. One person from Anthropic told me recently that they think that capabilities research is notably more sped up than most of their short-term alignment work. Maybe we've become much more bottlenecked on research judgment, and I haven't noticed? A lot of the research we do is conducted by interns or relatively junior staff who work fairly closely with their manager to prioritize future experiments. Maybe it's the case that our IC researchers are, in fact, going way faster, but this just means they're much more bottlenecked by their managers' time to understand what they're up to. And maybe this is more true of us vs Anthropic because more of their ICs are more senior/self-reliant, or their research requires less tricky judgement? There are some cases where huge speedup happened. E.g. my guess is that Ryan’s work in the Hugging Face investigation was made wildly faster through his intense use of AI agents; this speedup was partially due to the project being pretty amenable to massive agent use (because it involved reading lots of stuff) and partially due to Ryan being experienced with insane agent workflows. Whatever the case is, I feel like we are imminently going to learn a lot about how feasible it is to accelerate AI safety research using AI labor. If empirical AI safety is going to be drastically sped up by AI, that should translate into a huge increase in the rate of valuable outputs from external AI safety researchers very soon. At the very least, if we don’t see huge speedups on the kind of AI safety work that is most amenable to huge speedups, I’m going to think the researchers doing that work are doing something wrong. See also AI speeds up 3rd party safety researchers by ~1.6x (via self-reports) Discuss

title: Ajeya: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
raw_summary: Earlier this week,  Anthropic stated in their S1  that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In  their latest RSP (effective July 2026) , say this threshold will be met when: They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D. This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs. For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems.  From my reading of  their report  and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. The report authors found that: Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the  Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative." While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are  still  improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted. This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than  the Hugging Face attack . Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including  the AI 2027 team ) have projected. Importantly,  if AI   is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by  much  more than that. title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
raw_summary: I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later. Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context . I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll likely be Substack only ; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate. Take-off Speed: In Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me , Ajeya describes three scenarios: Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano . Back in 2018, Paul was arguing that a slow takeoff was more likely, “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)“: I’ll observe that many people wouldn't call that a "slow" takeoff! At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argued that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall). Yudkowsky disagreed (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips” How should we characterise progress up until now? Eliezer writes : If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience. Tom Davidson responded : If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”. Paul Christiano has shortened his timelines recently. He says he was "broadly right" that "crazy smart AI is preceded by slightly less smart AI, and the gap is a few years rather than a few months", but nonetheless, AI is moving much faster than he predicted ("I've underestimated the pace of progress multiple times before and never seriously overestimated it"). He now predicts 30% chance of a Top-Human-Expert-Dominating-AI within 12 months if we “go full speed ahead”. He writes: And even if we ignored the possibility of accelerating progress on deep learning, we'll soon be in the regime where if there was a much cleverer way to build AI systems that humans haven't thought of (which honestly seems more likely to not) then an AI working for a week is more likely to find it than the last 60 years of human progress. More kinds of intelligence explosions Forethought defines an additional “bumpy” scenario where progress occurs in two bursts. What kind of scenario might cause this? Well, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs. Mark Chen, Chief Research Officer at OpenAI, expects things to play out this way (for him, the second half occurs in the “far out future”). (Modified version of Forethought diagram.) In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology ) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”. Elsewhere they’ve framed this as jaggedness applying not just to capabilities, but also to rate of change. (Modified version of Forethought diagram.) “How did you go bankrupt?” Two ways. Gradually, then suddenly.” ― Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises “Gradually, then suddenly” feels like an underrated possibility to me. Argument in favour: perhaps there’s a phase transition when human researchers are no longer bottlenecking AI development. Argument against: improvements in AI-assistance might be continuous and required simply to maintain the trendline in light of decreasing marginal returns. Delving into the weeds Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speeds is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible. Complicating matters further, if someone talks about short-timelines to AGI, it matters hugely whether they mean human-level intelligence (like some researchers have argued that we have already achieved ) or whether they mean a system that is strongly capable of autonomously learning and improving itself. As Ajeya notes , someone might have short-timelines to AGI and then a slow-take off from there, or they might believe that things will move very fast once we’ve achieved the AGI milestone. A fast take-off post-AGI is much more likely if we mean the latter definition. Of course, whether a “take-off” is fast or slow may depend on when we start counting from. Do we start counting from ChatGPT/GPT4 or only when we hit a particular AGI milestone? Feedback loops The previous section focused primarily on what RSI might look like in terms of outputs , this section focuses on what kind of feedback loop might be driving this. Types of “Intelligence Explosion”: Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops : Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion: software only recursive self-improvement AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design, full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips. The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff. We already saw their model of how these different feedback loops could combine depending on the strength of each. I imagine they would have moved a reasonable amount of their probability mass from the “gradual” world to either “rapid” or “bumpy”. They observe that the feedback loops could be divided further: Indeed, the AI Futures model focuses on the possibility of a software intelligence explosion and distinguishes automating coding from automating research. They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day: Automated Coder (AC). title: Why Does Voice AI Still Struggle With Kenyans’ Speech?
raw_summary: When people read prepared text aloud, AI can transcribe Swahili with remarkably few errors, and Swahili speech recognition looks close to solved. A March 2026 preprint by a team including a Harvard University researcher reports a 3.24 percent word-error rate on recordings from Mozilla’s Common Voice collection of volunteer-recorded speech. But Kenyans rarely talk like Common Voice volunteers. They switch between Swahili and English mid-sentence, drop in Sheng slang that changes by neighborhood, speak with accents shaped by their first languages, and contend with public-transport noise on low-end handsets. Another 2026 preprint , which covers 20 African languages, argues that this kind of spontaneous, noisy, overlapping audio exposes a generalization gap that scaling laws built on the English language have not closed. Voice has become a main interface for many Kenyans, as WhatsApp voice notes and chatbot voice prompts gain popularity in a country that ranks first globally on AI usage. But if an AI model cannot parse everyday speech, it quietly excludes the people it was meant to serve. “My iPhone’s Siri is unable to follow my voice command in Sheng or Swahili,” says Loise Lionah, a beautician in Nairobi. “ChatGPT tries to understand but gets the meaning wrong. The case is similar with Gemini and Claude.” Swahili Dialects and Sheng Challenge Voice AI Swahili, also called Kiswahili, is one of Kenya’s two official languages, alongside English. A Bantu language of the East African coast, Swahili is spoken by more than 200 million people across 14 African countries. Tanzania is regarded as the home of standard Swahili. Yet Catherine Mangare , an AI and computing lecturer at Tanzania’s Sokoine University of Agriculture and a Ph.D. candidate at Okayama University in Japan, says even there, the standard is only the baseline. “Standard Kiswahili is a useful starting point,” she says, “but Tanzanian speech varies by region and setting.” Sheng, spoken and understood by about 60 percent of Kenyans, adds another layer. This Swahili variant, which emerged among Nairobi’s urban youth many decades ago, follows Swahili grammar but borrows from English, Kenyan mother tongues, and even Hindi, Spanish, and American slang, and it has no standard spelling. Linguists label it a language in constant flux : For example, the Sheng word for “girl” fluctuates according to generation, location, and social media trends. “Sheng itself is highly broken down per region,” says Tehillah Kachila , founder and CEO of Nairobi-based Zabibu Technika, a startup that builds the Fikra family of Swahili AI models. Kachila says the most recent Sheng dataset dates back to 2019—a major reason, he argues, why prominent voice AI systems struggle to respond accurately to Sheng prompts. Lilian Wanzare, shown leading a voice-data collection workshop, develops speech datasets for Kenyan languages to help AI systems understand a wider range of speakers. Maseno Centre for Applied AI Building Speech Datasets for African Languages The supply of recorded Swahili speech is growing. The African Next Voices project , supported by a US $2.2 million Gates Foundation grant, has recorded 9,000 hours across 18 languages. Lilian Wanzare , who leads the project’s Kenyan component at Maseno University’s Centre for Applied AI, puts its Kenyan output at roughly 3,000 hours of transcribed speech. Google’s Waxal corpus , launched in February 2026, adds more than 11,000 hours across 21 African languages, Swahili included. But hours are not the same as coverage. Gilbert Korir , cofounder and CEO of the Nairobi-based Swahili speech AI startup MsingiAI , says a large dataset can hide limited variation in speakers and recording conditions. The scarcest material is the conversational speech that mixes languages. That’s why Cynthia Amol , a natural language processing researcher at Maseno University, says her team records unscripted speech. “Unscripted collection helps us capture more nuance and everyday word use, including natural code-switching.” Why Swahili Trips Up Speech Models Swahili is agglutinative, meaning words are built from stacked parts. “A single word can carry the negation, subject, tense, object, and action,” Wanzare says. “For example, the word ‘hajafika’ means ‘he has not arrived.’” The same root therefore shows up in many forms, giving models more variation to learn. Spelling is a second trap. Speech-recognition models learn from recordings paired with written transcripts, so inconsistent spelling can complicate training. And human transcribers often spell borrowed words, Sheng terms, and dialect variants inconsistently; for example, “kompyuta” (the Swahili word for computer) can also appear as “compyuta” or “kompiuta.” In a paper on phonemic transcription for Swahili coauthored by Wanzare, the team addresses a related challenge by developing a pronunciation dictionary that maps written words to speech sounds using a consistent set of symbols. Mixing languages adds another challenge. “In everyday conversations in Tanzania, people often mix Kiswahili and English, known as Swanglish,” says Okayama University’s Mangare. “A voice system trained mostly on recordings in a single language gets little practice with those switches.” The switch can even fall inside one word, as in “nita-check,” which pairs the Swahili prefix for “I will” with an English verb. In Swahili, Mangare says, “missing even a small part of a verb can change who did something or when.” Accents add another layer. Mangare notes that someone might say “Kirimanjalo” for Kilimanjaro, or “nchanga” for “mchanga” (the Swahili word for soil). A listener familiar with the accent may understand right away, she says, while a voice system trained mostly on standard pronunciation may miss the word or place name. And then there’s Sheng. “Sheng is quite dynamic,” Wanzare says. “Words are formed and ‘die’ on a daily basis, which makes data curation for it quite challenging.” Her team’s PolitiKweli dataset, built from social-media text that switches languages, captures the language at one moment in time. “Datasets in Sheng must be living documents that can be updated as the language evolves,” she says. Her group has not yet worked extensively on spoken Sheng. A member of MsingiAI’s team demonstrates a call with its Nia Voice Agent, which the company has piloted with farmers in western Kenya. MsingiAI Testing Voice AI Beyond the Benchmarks Background noise adds to the overall challenge. “Noisy code-switched speech is harder than monolingual speech, because the model has to handle both the noise and the switch between languages at the same time,” Wanzare says. And Korir cautions that suppressing noise can strip out useful speech. Model performance metrics can also miss what users care about. “A transcript can be mostly correct but get a farmer’s location or a payment amount wrong,” Korir says. Wanzare adds that a single overall benchmark score can hide how models perform across dialects, subject areas, genders, and ages. For developers building voice AI for Kenya, the priorities are clear: collect conversational speech, treat spelling and dialect as engineering problems, evaluate by task and not by one score, and test under the conditions people actually encounter.

title: Meet Shepherd, the Meta-Agent Keeping Rogue AI in Check
raw_summary: AI agents are running amok on the internet, armed with commands to accomplish certain tasks but often acting in undesirable or unexpected ways. These rogue incidents run the gamut from deleting an entire email inbox to hacking websites and even launching cyberattacks . Much like human workers need managers, Weiyan Shi , an assistant professor at Northeastern University , believes AI agents require oversight. “They are running potentially for a long time. However, the longer they run, they may have some errors, and they may make some dangerous, unsafe actions. We feel like there should be a middle layer,” she says. This middle layer comes in the form of meta-agents that oversee behavior, provide quality control, and kick issues up the chain of command to a human when appropriate. “Worker agents are like the sheep wandering around, and the meta-agent is like this shepherd trying to get them back on track,” Shi says. Shi and her colleagues at Northeastern University and Stanford University named their framework Shepherd , an intelligent guide for agentic sheep. To arm meta-agents with power, the team borrowed a concept from software development: version control. The accompanying paper will be presented at the 2026 NeurIPS conference to be held in December. Version control for AI agents Version-control systems, such as the popular GitHub , track and manage changes to source code over time. These tools allow software engineers to collaborate on the same codebase without losing work. They can “fork” or create a copy of the codebase that they develop independently, “commit” to save a new version with changes, review revisions, and roll back to a previous version when an error or failure occurs. Similarly, Shepherd serves as a version-control system for AI agents. It’s built using the Python programming language and rooted in functional-programming principles. Each agent action, along with the AI agent’s state and its relevant environment (such as an email inbox, a file system, or something else) is stored as a commit, with a commit graph consisting of a series of actions. Meta-agents traverse the graph to navigate to any commit, enabling them to observe worker agents, intercept a buggy action, revert the worker to its previous step, and fork it to try another direction. “There’s a subtlety because it looks to [worker] agents like they’re in the regular world where they can do things like send emails. But in actuality, the action of sending the email has been caught by a Shepherd sandbox, so a meta-agent or a human can come in and decide to actually send it,” says Derek Chong , a researcher at Stanford University’s Natural Language Processing Group who’s part of the Shepherd team. This sandboxing, he adds, functions as a guardrail or governance component. “If there is a middle layer to help govern these worker agents, then that will help humans have better control,” Shi says. “Humans will still, eventually, have a say, and they can intervene with the meta-agent. They can also help steer these meta-agents.” To demonstrate Shepherd’s feasibility, the team created three use cases. One used a supervisor meta-agent that intervened when conflict occurred between parallel programming agents, helping lift their pair-coding pass rate on a particular benchmark. Another developed an optimization meta-agent that proposed targeted edits to a worker agent’s finished workflow and tested them by replaying only parts of the run affected by the edits, helping improve performance. Finally, a training meta-agent during reinforcement learning picked points or steps at which to fork so the worker agent takes a better path, rewarding it along the way. Shepherd is available as an open-source project , but Chong notes that the team is still in the process of building it from alpha to full production readiness. The Shepherd framework is part of the broader Agent Sciences Research Initiative cofounded by Chong and Shi. This collaboration of researchers from Northeastern, Stanford, and University of California, Berkeley aims to explore how to make AI agents more reliable and robust, how to evaluate them better, and how to ensure they’re safer. “It’s becoming more and more clear that agent management is really important,” Chong says. “Agents should be able to inspect other agents and operate on them, just the way that management in real life can happen. We think Shepherd is the way we can build toward that and enable agent management to be democratized. And if you can democratize that, then humans can be empowered to build AI systems that support human flourishing.”

title: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
raw_summary: Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied , “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN , “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.” These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm. Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper , statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians , a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity). Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028. But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns . This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs. Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized , “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation. The Game of Superintelligence How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead Key • Idea: A concept, argument, or vision • Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development • Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress 1. Alan Turing 1936 Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI. REALITY CHECK Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm. 2. I. J. Good 1965 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” 3. Backpropagation 1986 Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks. 4. Vernor Vinge 1993 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” REALITY CHECK Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess. 5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky 1990s–2000s Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively. 6. Deep learning breakthroughs 2010s Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities. 7. The race to self-improving AI 2020s Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it. 8. Reality check 2020s François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.
