title: Startup Makes Headway Toward Formalizing All of Math With AI
raw_summary: As Axiom Math ’s AI swarm was putting the final touches on the automatic verification of a 15,000-page proof of the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) , colloquially referred to as the “enormous theorem,” on Sunday, 25 October, the company’s Founding Mathematician Ken Ono had nothing to do but watch and reflect on the achievement. As the son of a mathematician , he had grown up surrounded by some of the architects of the CFSG’s proof, widely considered to be the longest mathematical proof ever written by humans. Now, he was contributing to formally verifying what his father and peers had created. “My wife was with me as I watched the team countdown to completing the verification,” he recalls. “God, I cannot tell you how emotional I was.” University of St Andrews group theorist Colva Roney-Dougal (who was not involved in the work) says of formalizing CFSG: “I held it up as an example of something that was going to be incredibly hard to formalize because I had thought that the amount of computing it was going to require was just unattainable,” she says. “So when I heard the announcement, I was really, really surprised.” This result, along with the concurrent formal verification of the 7,500-page Stacks project , represent a huge AI engineering achievement and lay some of the groundwork for digitizing all mathematics. Formally Enormous Why the hoo-ha? The CFSG concerns finite simple groups. These are groups (sets of elements combined with an operation, like addition or multiplication, that follows specific rules) that are simple (in other words, cannot be reduced or simplified further) and finite (as opposed to groups containing an infinite number of elements). For example, all the permutations of a deck of cards form a simple finite group. Évariste Galois laid the foundations for group theory almost 200 years ago. Finite simple groups have since been classified by myriad mathematicians into 18 families (plus 26 sporadic simple groups that do not belong to any of these families). The CFSG’s proof confirms that this list is complete. But this simple task was achieved only by bringing together results and arguments that far exceed what any individual mathematician can fully absorb from more than 500 journal articles written by around 100 authors over a half-century period. Translating this interconnected web of knowledge into code and verifying its correctness therefore posed a number of significant engineering challenges, even beyond those overcome in earlier proof formalizations by Axiom Math this year . One of the hardest, according to Axiom Math’s Niels Voss , who led the CFSG formalization, was the sheer length of the proof. Over 15,000 pages of dense mathematics, the CFSG proof contains multiple theorems, lemmas, and definitions none of which can be checked until everything has been made machine-readable. To get around this required some ingenuity. “We processed all the literature from the CFSG and traced the network structure of the informal proof before we were able to start working on it,” says Voss. “We then broke up the statement of the CFSG into about 100 milestones—landmark results along the way that can be independently verified—which we used to guide the formalization and stay on track.” Roney-Dougal says she is very impressed with the result and particularly appreciates how the formal proof finds and clears up several mistakes in the original human proof. She thinks this result is critical to formalizing any modern research in group theory, such as her own work understanding how simple finite groups behave. But, Roney-Dougal says, because the verification was done automatically, there are few mathematicians capable of extracting information from the proof to share with the community, and that a new generation of mathematicians may have “missed a chance to gain knowledge from the doing of it.” Stacks of Ingenuity Required Just nine days after the CFSG formalization announcement, Axiom Math revealed it had automatically formalized the Stacks project, too. Started in 2005 by Columbia University mathematician Aise Johan de Jong , Stacks is a massive, open-source collaborative mathematics textbook and reference work focused on highly abstract algebraic geometry and algebraic stacks (geometric spaces that are vital to modern string theory and number theory). Whereas CFSG is a single (huge) landmark theorem, the Stacks project is essentially a well-structured library of thousands of interlocking definitions, constructions, and lemmas bringing all of modern algebraic geometry together. The final Stacks formalization stands at a mere 16 million lines of code (compared to CFSG’s 43 million lines of code, roughly on a par with the Linux kernel), but it presented a different challenge to Axiom Math engineers: needing to achieve faithfulness and coherence across thousands of interlocking definitions and theorems, says Axiom Math’s Vasily Ilin , who led the project. This required the team to design a hierarchical system of AI agents with specialized responsibilities working in parallel, keeping every definition aligned across the library, while also checking faithfulness with multiagent audits, cross-checks against sources, and hard tests. This ensured that every element and task aligned across the entire project. A highly efficient, general, reusable, and maintainable formal library of foundational concepts underpinning much of modern mathematics, the impact of the Stacks formalization could be profound. Now, anyone or any bot can access the formal Stacks library and build new formal mathematics upon it. And together, the CFSG and Stacks formalizations represent a significant step toward formalizing all of mathematics. “They show the two ways formalization has to scale: one very long proof, and one very wide body of connected theory,” says Ono. Ono and Voss see numerous advantages to a future in which formal mathematics becomes central: rubber-stamping theorems and proofs, preserving knowledge as expertise dwindles over time, and building a shared library as a basis for creating new mathematics. They are also optimistic about humanity’s role when all of mathematics is formalized, viewing formalization as a launchpad for humans to use and understand mathematics in new and innovative ways. “Aren’t we excited to think more broadly about what the future of math can be?” asks Ono. “I’m excited by that. I’m really excited.”

title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
raw_summary: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous and intelligent systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote. A suite of standards The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD ’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process ( IEEE 7000-2021 ), AI system transparency ( IEEE 7001-2021 ), data privacy ( IEEE 7002-2022 ), algorithmic bias considerations ( IEEE 7003 -2024), the impact on people’s well-being ( IEEE 7010-2020 ), machine-readable personal privacy requirements ( IEEE 7012-2025 ), and systems that mimic human empathy ( IEEE 7014-2024 ). AI ethics certifications IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd , which includes two certifications : one for individuals and one for products. The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program , which can certify it and issue the certification mark. IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program . This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements. New industry connections group The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members. The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle. The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability. Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues. “The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.” Podcasts and blogs To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “ Ethically Aligned Design : 10 Years of Impact” podcast series . It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks. The episodes center around the vision for EAD , the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards. The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices. The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems. The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog articles about the IEEE 7000 series and educational resources to continue to raise awareness and support of this groundbreaking work. This article was updated on 18 November 2026.

title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
raw_summary: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N 2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N 2 . In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N , not N 2 . So the energy used will scale as N , not N 2 , as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied. Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10 -19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10 -14 and 10 -12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000. But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements. McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.” It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law . “Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.” With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data. Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains. Bridging the gap in free space The startup Lumai , based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr , declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs. Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. title: AI Companies Develop Decision Models to Avoid Hallucinations
raw_summary: On 15 September, a startup called TypeSafe AI released a new AI model called Jev . The company’s broad, disruptive claims about Jev turned heads: The company claimed that Jev, which it calls a “System One model” is cheaper, faster, and can’t hallucinate. TypeSafe AI’s marketing is an obvious shot across the bow of other AI companies and their large language models (LLMs), which, despite their capabilities in math and coding, are infamous for their cost and tendency to “hallucinate” factually incorrect replies. And the startup has certainly attracted both attention and investment. The company recently raised US $870 million in funding at a valuation of $7.5 billion . But the most impressive metric of Jev’s success is arguably the many imitators it’s already spawned. Amazon, Cloudflare, Microsoft, and OpenAI quickly released “decision models” that imitate Jev’s capabilities. Startups, academic researchers, and independent enthusiasts have released dozens more. “I have to give Jev credit,” says Matt Mastracci , an independent developer who has trained and released several decision models including Djev , which Cloudflare cited as an inspiration for its own decision models . “It really brought decision models to the forefront. In six or seven weeks, we’ve seen dozens of models come out.” Jev’s Latency and Compute Advantages Most AI researchers would call Jev a decision model or decider model. TypeSafe AI’s branding of Jev as a System One model refers to a theory of cognition popularized by psychologist Daniel Kahneman in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2013). In the book, Kahneman draws a line between fast, instinctive thought (System One) and slower, deliberate thought (System Two). TypeSafe AI argues that modern LLMs offer the second, but are too slow to provide the first. The company claims that Jev can provide end-to-end response latency between 70 and 500 milliseconds. By comparison, LLMs typically require at least several seconds, to provide a response, and more complicated tasks (like coding software from scratch) can take several hours. Independent testing backs up TypeSafe AI’s claims. A preprint coauthored by Ramayya Krishnan , a professor of information systems at Carnegie Mellon University, along with several colleagues, found that Jev delivered a median latency of 150 ms across several benchmarks designed to gauge decision accuracy, including RewardBench and JudgeBench . OpenAI’s most capable model at the time, GPT-6 Astra, delivered a median latency of 1.89 seconds. A faster reply is often a cheaper reply, because it requires less compute time, and that’s reflected in TypeSafe AI’s pricing. The startup charges $0.042 per million input tokens; output tokens are free. By contrast, for GPT-6 Astra, ChatGPT charges $10 per million input tokens; $50 per million output tokens. Even GPT-6 Luna, a variant of GPT-6 designed for fast, inexpensive inference, costs $0.10 per million input tokens; $0.50 per million output tokens . Mastracci says that lower latency and costs open opportunities to tackle tasks LLMs currently can’t handle.“You can think of content moderation, such as moderating a fire hose of social media posts or an extremely busy chat room.” Michelle Chen , a group product manager at Cloudflare (which has released its own decision models, including Clef and Claric ), is also bullish on what decision models can accomplish. “You can probably offload 80 percent of your typical LLM tasks to a System One model that is going to be so much faster and so much cheaper.” TypeSafe AI has offered few details about how Jev achieves its speed, but Jev’s open-weights imitators provide more transparency. For example, take Cloudflare’s Clef, an open-weights decision model which is free to download on Hugging Face . “With an LLM, when you’re generating an output token, it looks at all the previous tokens and predicts the next output token,” explains Chen. This occurs in sequence, token after token, until an end token is reached. “Our decision models don’t do that. They just do a single forward pass, to generate one read of all the inputs, and then generate one output. That’s why it’s a lot faster.” How Decision Models Generalize Tasks Decision models based on an LLM, such as Clef (which is based on Alibaba’s Qwen LLM ), still contain the neurons and transformer-based model architecture of an LLM. They still input and output tokens. However, the portions of the model that turn these tokens into text have been changed to constrain the output. “Jev can only answer questions with a predefined, structured answer format,” says Zhongyu Wei , a professor at Fudan University, in Shanghai, who is also a coauthor of a study that benchmarks decision models and introduces an open-weight alternative, SII-Decision . “We give it a question and options such as A, B, and C, and it must choose from those options, returning probabilities alongside its choice.” In one sense, decision models are a return to classifiers , a type of model that, as the name implies, learn to sort data into classes. They’re used in a wide range of tasks, including spam filters and face detection. “These kinds of models are not new,” says Chen. “It’s almost like a rebranding.” But decision models offer a key upgrade over prior classifiers: generalization. Independent developer Mastracci explains that classifiers were traditionally created through domain-specific training. Decision models, though, retain the general intelligence of an LLM, and that makes them applicable to many situations. “You can pick it up off the shelf, you point it at your problem, and it works,” says Mastracci. Cloudflare is putting this advantage into practice. Before decision models, teams looking to use a classifier model had to “get a lot of data, stand up a machine learning team, and fine-tune” a model for the task, Chen says. Decision models eliminate this requirement, so one decision model can be used in many domains. Examples include flagging spam pull requests in Cloudflare’s GitHub documentation repository, catching spam and phishing emails, spotting phishing domains, detecting prompt-injection attacks on LLMs, and reading emails about internet-backbone outages to judge whether they’ll affect Cloudflare’s services. Decision models are well suited for quick judgements on data like emails, messages, or documents. Source: TypeSafe AI Do Decision Models Really Stop Hallucinations? In programming, “type-safe” languages are designed so that operations mixing incompatible kinds of data—adding a number to a string, say—are rejected before the program runs rather than producing a bad result later. Decision models are similar in that they prevent the model from generating an unexpected reply. TypeSafe AI’s name makes the connection between type-safe programming and decision models part of the company’s marketing, and it builds on that to make a startling claim: Jev will never hallucinate. This is, strictly speaking, true. LLMs hallucinate because they calculate probabilities for tokens repeatedly across a huge vocabulary of possibilities and output many tokens. This leaves room for less probable tokens to lead a response astray, or for the model to deliver tokens that are probable based on the model’s training but not correct in the context of the reply. Decision models, by contrast, calculate probabilities only among the predetermined possibilities, and the most probable is chosen. This eliminates hallucination. However, Carnegie Mellon’s Krishnan cautions that “eliminating hallucinations in the output does not eliminate errors in decision-making.” He and his coauthors tested Jev by asking it to determine if answers to questions were correct. Jev performed well when the judgment could be easily reached by reading the prompt, but performance dropped off when the judgment required math or involved a logic puzzle. Wei of Fudan University and his coauthors report similar results in their own resear…

title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
raw_summary: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change. For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “ Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On .”

title: I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again
raw_summary: In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity. I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them. In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be. The Forensic Approach to Deepfake Detection Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.” Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it. I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.) I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second. A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory. Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters. My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real. But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view. This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake. Signaling a Video’s Provenance When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do? The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording. Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID , embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin. Apple recently took these ideas a step further . On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed. These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be. Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.” Real-Time Verification This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls. In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again. All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop. This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes. Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts , such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them. Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered i…

title: Systems and Software Outages Explained: Who or What Is Responsible?
raw_summary: Last Thursday, Microsoft 365’s Exchange Online and related apps like Outlook and Teams went down in at least 74 countries. The next day the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a full nationwide ground stop. Every airport in the United States stopped sending planes into the sky, and those already in the air had to come back down. On Monday, Chase Bank customers couldn’t get into their accounts for the better part of the day. Then United Airlines suffered an outage. And on Tuesday, the U.S. National Security Agency ’s classified communications network went down. Social media is flooded with conspiracy theories. Talking heads on television and YouTube are blaming everything from nefarious foreign governments to rogue AI agents. For a sober and sobering perspective on this, I turned to former IEEE Spectrum contributing editor Robert N. Charette . He spent the last two decades meticulously analyzing software and systems failures around the globe. No one is better equipped to explain the whys and hows of this parade of horribles to a world waking up to the fact that the infrastructure that undergirds modern life is being held together with the digital equivalent of duct tape and chewing gum. Is this just a bad couple of weeks or is it the new normal? Bob Charette has tracked and diagnosed software and system problems for decades. Robert N. Charette Robert N. Charette: Oh, I think it’s a bad week, but at the same time, it’s also the new normal. What I mean by that is that over the last 20 years of reporting for IEEE Spectrum , I have documented hundreds of outages over the years, and those are just the ones that come to the surface. In a typical week globally, there are hundreds of these glitches, but they’re just not reported–or if they are, they only make the local news. But these latest events are piled together, and so everybody’s supersensitive to them. And they are not minor. Friday’s nationwide ground stop was only the second since 9/11. And this current spate of failures actually goes back a few weeks. On 28 October, we had the train crash in Spain because of a safety system that went down. Again, what occurred there wasn’t uncommon. To my mind, none of these are uncommon. What is uncommon is that they’re clustered together. If you go back to last October and November, we had a cluster of outages as well. So this isn’t like the first time this has happened. And it’s not going to be the last time, either. The FAA Ground Stop Let’s break these down and look at some of these incidents in depth, starting with the ground stop on Friday. In his initial assessment, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said outdated communications equipment had been overloaded with data and went down . He later described a newly installed router that was sending a flood of connection attempts every few seconds, swamping other routers . That new router was being installed by the contractor L3Harris, which was replacing copper wire with fiber at a facility in southern Arkansas. What was your first reaction when you heard about this situation? Charette: That somebody didn’t do their homework. If you’re taking a look at what happened with the network, they were replacing old Cisco routers with new Juniper routers. The old Cisco routers have been around for about 20 years, I think. They can’t handle as much traffic as a new router can, especially with fiber optics. So they were updating their routers, and they were going to be updating thousands of these things throughout the network, which is run by L3Harris , right? It’s not run by the FAA. It’s contracted out. After the national ground stop, United Airlines had another stop due to its own IT problems. Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle/Getty Images Putting my engineering hat on, I believe that it’s probably an old router that had some peculiar fixes to actually make it work a long time ago. And so when they brought the new router in with the configuration that they had been using elsewhere—because they’ve installed 400 so far without a problem, with 69 operational—when they installed this one, there was something unique about it and it crashed the system. And so the crashing of the system was actually crashing the old network, the old Cisco routers, not the new ones. I believe that they’re going to find out, just like in 2009, when this sort of thing happened before , is that they didn’t do the right configuration management. They didn’t have a full understanding of the network, and they didn’t understand that particular set of circumstances at that particular location. The interesting thing to me is that the Arkansas location, which was the center point of the problem, and another router in Amarillo, Texas, started pinging back and forth with each other. I’m curious about how that actually happened as well. Because the one in Amarillo was installed, I think, three weeks ago without a problem. It’s always something weird that nobody thought about. So does that indicate a contractor oversight issue, like people at the FAA not keeping tabs on L3Harris? Charette: It’s partly an issue with the FAA. It’s partly an issue with L3Harris. It’s partly a consequence of the complexity of these systems that we have. Expecting every Cisco router you’re replacing to have exactly the same specs is asking a heck of a lot. You’re making a lot of assumptions. And as I wrote in my very last article before I retired from Spectrum , assumptions you make are risks you take. And I think they made a lot of assumptions about how the old routers were working and how they could configure them and do a plug and replace. That doesn’t happen. And you know, back 25 or 30 years ago, there would have been a lot more care in the test bed. I’m also interested in what happened at the L3Harris test bed at the simulation-stimulation lab that they used in Melbourne, Fla., and to see how robust it was to deal with these types of problems. But that said, it could have just been somebody just didn’t do the update, like they didn’t do it in 2009. Somebody turned something off and was supposed to turn it back on, and they didn’t. The FAA recently expanded an AI-based traffic tool called SMART to some of its facilities, and people on social media pointed at that as the culprit. The FAA and the tool’s developer both denied it had anything to do with the outage. This raises a broader question about the impact of AI on software maintenance. Is what we’re seeing a harbinger of things to come? Charette: The pessimist in me says yes , because if you take a look at where AI is being used and how it’s being paid for within organizations and within government, they’re taking it not out of new capital spend but out of legacy systems’ operational maintenance. So can I point to this incident being a result of that? I doubt it. But I think what you will likely see is that there’s going to be this giant race between deploying AI—which hopefully will increase network and system resilience—versus stealing from the money you need to keep the lights on in these legacy systems. Because if we leave aside the AI component for the moment and just look at the FAA network, this is a classic case where you’re putting in new hardware that has to communicate with legacy systems, and it’s that physical hardware and the software routing that has problems. Now if you take AI and bolt that onto legacy systems you probably don’t know very well, then you’re going to start seeing problems. It would not surprise me that we’re going to see an increase in failures as we start to move more AI into these systems. One of my old risk maxims is that the risk exists at the interfaces, and we don’t know these interfaces very well at all. There’s a big gap between what people know about their architectures and what they should know about their architectures. Microsoft 365 Goes Down Let’s pivot to the Microsoft outage. On Thursday, 12 November, Microsoft 365’s Exchange Online and related apps like Out…

title: These Engineers Are Cleaning Up Connected Cars’ Security Flaws
raw_summary: Today’s connected vehicles collect and transmit far more personal data from drivers and passengers than their predecessors, with costly consequences. The Center for Automotive Management in Germany estimates that cyberattacks have caused more than US $20 billion in damage to the auto industry as of 2025, twenty times as high as in 2022. This week, engineers and cybersecurity researchers are gathering in Bonn, Germany, for the Embedded Security in Cars (Escar) conference to discuss using AI for defense, hardening chips, and otherwise securing the auto industry’s data handling. Frank Kargl , an Escar Europe co-organizer and director of the Institute of Distributed Systems at Ulm University, in Germany, says that recent cyberattacks on infrastructure like supermarket refrigerators all over Europe have highlighted the risk of a broad hack of automobiles that aims to cause arbitrary damage . Kargl says the risk for a regular driver being singled out for hacking is still low, but “I think we still need to consider the case of large-scale attacks affecting massive numbers of vehicles and be prepared for this.” Lightweight data monitoring and firewalls to secure vehicle data Safeguarding a modern vehicle is no easy task. Cameras, microphones, GPS trackers, and other sensors capture a great deal of personal information, ranging from a person’s private conversations to their daily travel habits. That data is beamed across communications networks to data centers. Automakers sell some data to third-party companies. Each link is subject to cyberattack, and each software update could let in a new vulnerability. In response, engineers are developing adaptive, AI-enabled software defenses, building more-secure automotive chips, and battening down the entire network of infrastructure, ranging from aftermarket accessories to electric-vehicle charging stations. Kargl says that engineers are also working on migrating automobile cryptography to postquantum algorithms, because sooner or later quantum computers will be able to break traditional encryption methods. Computer scientist Olaf Landsiedel , of the Institute for Networked Cyber-Physical Systems at Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, is giving a keynote at the Escar conference about adaptive AI for automotives. He says that the future of auto cybersecurity will be lightweight systems that continuously monitor a vehicle’s communication in the background, pulling in a sophisticated AI model activated when suspicious behavior is observed. “This could provide more comprehensive monitoring without continuously consuming significant computational resources,” he says, which is necessary because cars have limited onboard computing power and energy. Landsiedel and colleagues have developed a deep-learning model they call “ThinkingViT” that uses a nested progressive-inference process to minimize the compute needed to accomplish image-recognition tasks. Detroit auto cybersecurity firm Block Harbor is borrowing design principles from enterprise IT, as they seek to protect increasingly data-heavy cars, says COO André Weimerskirch . This involves a “defense-in-depth” approach, with multiple layers of security, with the assumption that any single security barrier could be breached, he says. Block Harbor is also using AI to help scan for vulnerabilities. Fleet operators face their own challenges: They must secure vehicles they didn’t design or manufacture. In Norway, public transport operator Ruter announced in 2025 that it is developing firewalls to help protect its bus fleet. It had discovered that the software on buses made by the Chinese company Yutong could be updated remotely, with the theoretical risk that an adversary could shut down the vehicles. Ruter acknowledged at the time that it would need to remain vigilant, as the next generation of buses is set to be “more integrated and harder to secure.” Landsiedel says the fleet operators must consider not only the vehicles themselves but also all the infrastructure they interact with, as well as the central fleet-management system. “Every connection creates potential vulnerabilities,” he says, which means fleet operators should consider “end-to-end security, including authenticated communication, access control, and the protection of cloud and edge infrastructure.” Automakers and their suppliers have been scrutinizing their supply chains to comply with U.S. Commerce Department restrictions on components and software from China and Russia. Harman Some of these risks are hard to address through technical measures alone, especially in the face of nation-state-sponsored attacks. The U.S. Commerce Department has banned the import of Chinese and Russian connected vehicles starting with model year 2027, and is prohibiting automakers from using software and key components designed in those countries. Countries in Europe have also been mulling bans. “I feel the responsibility to defend against nation-state attackers is a shared responsibility between the vehicle manufacturer and the government,” Weimerskirch says. Indeed, U.S. restrictions have influenced the design of Samsung Electronics subsidiary Harman Automotive ’s global offerings, says Harman head of solution architecture and cybersecurity lead Monica Mitchell. “We don’t want to bifurcate our solutions,” she says. Research, regulators, prosecutors rein in car-data brokers Researchers and regulators are also working to curb carmakers’ voluntary oversharing of data with third parties. At Northeastern University, a team of researchers recently announced the results of a study in which they captured the data traffic emitted from 19 car brands. They drove the cars into a Faraday tent to isolate the signals, and rerouted the cars’ internet traffic to networks that the team controlled. The researchers found that cars were sending data to companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft. They also found the cars’ companion apps were sending personal information like vehicle identification numbers (VINs), email addresses, and geolocation data. Nicole Zagson , a doctoral candidate in cybersecurity at Northeastern and a coauthor of the study, says that privacy agreements for connected vehicles tend to be opaque, making it difficult for car owners to understand how their data is being shared. One automaker, Honda, took action in response to the research, asking an analytics vendor to delete drivers’ location information and VINs. “There’s not enough scrutiny on what they are putting into these vehicles, because it’s so hard to study,” Zagson says. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state prosecutors have taken action as well. In October, General Motors agreed to pay $220 million to settle allegations brought by 36 attorneys general that it illegally sold consumers’ driving behavior and location information to data brokers, which resold it to insurance companies. GM finalized a settlement with the FTC over similar allegations in January. While individual drivers have limited control over their car’s cybersecurity, Landsiedel says they can reduce their exposure by keeping software updated, using strong passwords and multifactor authentication when available, and avoiding untrusted aftermarket devices.

title: Europe’s Digital Wallets May Be More Traceable Than Intended
raw_summary: Millions of European Union citizens should soon have access to digital wallets , as member states roll out their implementations of the European Digital Identity Regulation ahead of an end-of-the-year deadline. But the digital-identity wallets, which are intended to provide a secure and private place to store identifying information such as bank-account information, diplomas, and government IDs, such as driver’s licenses, could leave behind a trail of cryptographic clues that makes it possible to recognize someone across services. Cryptographers warn that the technology protecting individual privacy may not yet go far enough to stop people from being tracked. Advances in cryptographic techniques since the law was passed in 2024 means this problem could be solved. However, the law doesn’t require that these techniques be used, and cryptographers that IEEE Spectrum spoke with are split as to whether the wallets should be rolled out at all without such a requirement in place, and whether they’ll be secure enough without it. With digital wallets, when someone is asked to provide their ID, a digital, verifiable form of the ID can be transmitted, via a QR code for example. When scanned with a verification app, it would show basic identifying user information, according to Anna Lysyanskaya , a professor of computer science at Brown University. The EU’s digital-identity regulation already includes a requirement for selective disclosure, which allows people to share only the attributes requested by the person checking identification rather than handing over an entire document. A bar checking someone’s age, for example, could request a simple confirmation that a person is over 18 and not need their full name or address.. Tracking Risks in EU Digital Wallets When the person who requested the ID scans it, they still record some personal information, such as the digital signature and identifiers that are required to check the ID. This additional information can serve as a way of tracking a user even if the attributes shared are quite common. Two requesters could share this information to show they had interacted with the same person, says Johannes Schönrich , the director at the FIM Research Center for Information Management at the Augsburg Technical University of Applied Sciences, in Germany. If two parties can share that information, that would be a problem: EU legislation specifies that the wallets should also be unlinkable, which means that “tracking a user by means of [these] digital attestations should not be possible,” says Schönrich. One way to address the problem is to issue multiple versions of a user’s credentials, each with different cryptographic information attached, says Lysyanskaya. The wallet could keep track of which certificates have already been used, ensuring that a different one is presented during each interaction. “If you allow a service provider to say, Look, I’m not supporting the Google protocol, I want a traditional verification, you essentially allow the service provider to do a kind of downgrade.” —Jaap-Henk Hoepman, Radboud University This approach has limitations. If the issuer—the government department that creates and digitally verifies that the credential is authentic—can identify who a credential was originally issued to, it could potentially help link the different versions back to the same person, according to Lysyanskaya. “Now anybody you’ve ever interacted with has some kind of way of tracking you,” she says. “If this kind of interaction becomes really ubiquitous…then unless we place a tremendous amount of trust in both issuers and verifiers to guard our privacy, we may encounter a situation where everybody knows at all times what everybody else is up to, by just leaving these little digital crumbs of information about yourself.” Lysyanskaya was one of 16 cryptographers who were invited to provide feedback for the European Commission when the law was passed in 2024. They recommended using anonymous credentials, which use zero-knowledge proofs to let people demonstrate their identity or eligibility without revealing unnecessary personal information. How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Work Zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to convince another that something is true without needing to send any additional information beyond the fact that it is true. For example, they would allow someone to demonstrate that they hold a valid government-issued credential, or meet a particular requirement, without revealing the underlying personal information or creating the same linkable record of the interaction, says Lysyanskaya. If these two people, the person checking the ID and the person being asked for it ever meet again, there will be no record of any earlier encounters. The service provider could still verify that the credential is authentic, has not expired or been revoked, and has not been manipulated. However, it would receive less information than it does under traditional verification methods. “You learn exactly what you need, but not a single bit more about anything that might accidentally be disclosed but is not that necessary,” says Schönrich. Zero-knowledge proofs have existed in cryptography since the 1980s , but teams of researchers have only recently developed techniques to run them on more-constrained devices like smartphones. Shortly after the EU’s digital-wallet regulations were passed in 2024, for example, a research team at Google found a way to generate zero-knowledge proofs using credentials signed with the elliptic-curve digital-signature algorithm, which generates and authenticates digital signatures efficiently enough to be used in a digital wallet. Those kinds of credentials allow individuals to prove that a credential is valid without revealing the cryptographic signature that could otherwise make separate interactions linkable, according to Jaap-Henk Hoepman , an associate professor of computer science at Radboud University, in the Netherlands. The European Commission wants to conduct more research on implementing zero-knowledge proofs before making them a mandatory requirement for wallet operators from day 1. Because of that, it considers the proofs to be “a core road map item,” according to the universal digital blueprint for the wallets. EU governments are free to implement them on a by-country basis if they so choose. The Commission said on its GitHub page for the wallets that zero-knowledge proofs are not yet mandatory because “there is currently no clear, certifiable approach agreed at EU level,” and that it needs to do more pan-European consultation with cryptographers and groups, such as the European Cybersecurity Certification Group (ECCG), that oversee the profession. “Refinement at this stage focuses on establishing common understanding and boundaries, rather than immediate deployment to secure and privacy-preserving future integration,” the Commission’s GitHub post from June 2026 reads. Schönrich says he understands the Commission’s position, but wants them to commit to a binding timeline for introducing zero-knowledge proofs in the next few years for a second version of the wallets. Karsten Wildberger, Germany’s federal minister for digitalization and state modernization, unveils the country’s version of the European Union’s EUDI digital wallet in September 2026. Bernd von Jutrczenka/picture alliance/Getty Images Zero-Knowledge Proofs in EU Digital Wallets The cryptographers that Spectrum spoke with are split on whether the EU should ask states to roll out digital wallets without adding in zero-knowledge proofs. The regulation does not specify what type of cryptographic protocols should be used as each country implements its version of the digital wallet, just the privacy requirements. Hoepman argues that zero-knowledge proofs should be mandated by law so that wallets have to implement this technology. title: How Cozey turns its operators into software builders on Vercel
raw_summary: Employees outside engineering, including warehouse, finance, and support staff, are now building applications and deploying them to Vercel Finance uses an app it built to review profit and loss weekly instead of monthly Adopting Vercel Flags allowed Cozey to retire a separate tool that cost approximately $80,000 annually Six projects, including the storefront, use AI Gateway Cozey is a Canadian furniture company that makes modular sofas customers can configure for their homes. It runs its storefront and most of its back-office applications on Vercel. Warehouse, finance, and customer support employees now securely deploy their own apps on that same platform. Turning everyday problems into working applications CEO Fred Aubé encourages employees to solve problems they encounter without waiting for another team to take them on. Sam Morrison, VP of Digital, saw teams reach the limits of what they could prototype in an AI chat. Employees used coding agents to build web apps. With Vercel, they could deploy an app themselves and give coworkers a link to a working tool. In the warehouse, a coordinator built a live floor plan that shows where boxes sit and what staff are doing. Sam says engineering would not have prioritized that project. Finance built its own app to track profit and loss and now uses it to review performance every week instead of once a month. A customer support representative built an app that uses AI to generate images of Cozey furniture in a customer’s own room. In October, Cozey planned to make the tool available to shoppers. Sam says a new app appears almost every week. Extending Vercel from the storefront to the business behind it Sam estimates that the Atmosphere sofa collection alone has about 1.2 million possible configurations. Cozey worked with an agency specializing in Next.js to rebuild its storefront on Vercel. With a custom front end, the team could decide how shoppers explore those options. Cozey uses Fluid compute for functions on the storefront. It runs internal Python backends and the Cozey Operating System, or C.O.S., on Vercel. Teams use C.O.S. to forecast orders, manage warehouse and retail operations, review finances, and track business performance. Operating margin depends in part on how quickly furniture moves from incoming containers to customer shipments. Each C.O.S. pull request gets a Vercel Preview Deployment , giving the team a working application to test before release. Cozey’s engineers reported that with caching, builds on Vercel took a couple of minutes. They also share preview links with Fred so he can try changes and give feedback. The team uses Vercel Flags to control how new features reach users, replacing a separate tool that cost approximately $80,000 annually. After release, performance metrics on Vercel give the team a common reference for checking how applications are running. When Cozey launched in Australia, the team had regional backend work to do. For the storefront on Vercel, Sam says, “it wasn’t even a conversation.” Managing access as more people build As more employees began building, Cozey needed to manage who could open their applications and who could deploy and maintain them. An employee once deployed an app that anyone on the internet could open. For internal apps that had shipped without appropriate authentication, Sam turned on access protection on Vercel . “It saved us from some pretty serious privacy risks,” says Sam. Cozey uses single sign-on so members of its Vercel team can sign in with company credentials. The company manages team membership through groups in its employee directory with Directory Sync . Giving AI applications a common way to access models As more teams built with AI, Sam saw them repeating the work of connecting to models. Six Cozey projects, including the storefront, send model requests through Vercel AI Gateway . Cozey’s engineers use it to call models from their code editors, too. Sam wants all of Cozey’s model requests to go through Gateway. AI Gateway gives teams one interface for different model providers. If a provider is unavailable, the gateway can route the request to another provider that serves the same model. It adds no markup to provider token prices. Sam describes the added cost of routing requests through it as “basically $0 in additional overhead.” The company is also developing what it calls the Agentic Mesh, a system to coordinate AI use across internal applications and customer experiences. The coordinating service is being built on AWS, with AI Gateway planned for model requests and Vercel for application deployment. It is intended to help teams decide which models to use and where to run applications, while giving engineering visibility into AI usage and costs. What's next Sam says engineering wouldn’t have prioritized a live map of the warehouse floor. The coordinator who needed to see where the boxes were could make a different call, build the map, and share it with the people moving them. When the digital team sees an idea worth taking further, it has a working app to build on. Cozey chose a custom storefront on Vercel so it could decide how shoppers explore its furniture. Sam’s next goal is for employees outside engineering to share that control. If shoppers keep asking the same question about a sofa, the support rep who hears it could put the answer on the product page. Read more

title: Workflow is 10x faster, again
raw_summary: Workflow SDK 5.8 runs workflows on a new execution engine, rebuilt for performance. Step-to-step latency is 12x lower, and large fan-outs, like running 256 steps in parallel, use 14x less function time outside your step code. This directly improves turn times for durable AI agents , among many other improvements. To get the new engine, upgrade to workflow@5.8.0 or later. New runs will use the new engine by default, and runs already started on an older version will safely keep running on that version. Make sure your steps are idempotent where possible to get the most out of this upgrade. Drastically reduced overhead In our benchmarks comparing 5.2.0 to 5.8.0 , p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 85 ms to 7 ms. The median run, including 102 seconds of step work, finished in 111 seconds instead of 3.0 minutes. Running 256 parallel steps in a fan-out added 5.5× less overhead, 2.5 seconds instead of 13.5 seconds, and the median run spent 14× less time in functions beyond the steps' own work, 105 seconds instead of 1,446. A five-turn agent loop that streams its tokens through durable streams and calls tools added 0.9 seconds of overhead instead of 3.0 seconds, 3.3× less. Consult the benchmarks page for how we measure these numbers. Resuming after 1 second idle time went from 425 ms to 184 ms, 2.3× faster. Resumptions more than 5 seconds out might see slightly larger overhead. You can choose to keep functions warm for longer to optimize time-to-resume at the cost of additional compute time. Speculative execution for retryable steps Many of the above benefits rely on speculative execution of Steps. Only Steps that are idempotent can be run in this way. A step that passes its stepId as an idempotency key , like the Stripe charge below, is already safe and needs no changes. If your step is sensitive and can't be retried, mark it with maxRetries = 0 to opt out and ensure it still runs at most once. You should already be making Steps idempotent wherever possible, or flag them with maxRetries = 0 , to ensure Workflow SDK doesn't re-run your Steps when it's not safe to do so. Get started Upgrade to workflow@5.8.0 . To keep creating runs on the previous engine after upgrading, set WORKFLOW_SPEC_VERSION=8 . If you're on 4.x, start with the upgrade guide , since v5 is a major release. Using a third-party World? All Worlds maintained by Vercel already support the new engine. A third-party World needs to support World spec version 9 before upgrading gives you any of these improvements. Until it does, new runs keep using the previous engine. Read more

title: All Sandbox runtimes now use Vercel Managed Images
raw_summary: All Vercel Sandbox runtimes now use Vercel Managed Images (VMIs). Legacy runtimes, such as node22 , now use the open-source images in the vercel/sandbox repository , distributed through Vercel Container Registry (VCR). Sandboxes created with these now come with 64 GB of storage and use the same infrastructure as sandboxes powered by VCR. The universal image is released nightly, and rolling tags such as latest pick up operating system, dependency, and coding agent updates. Pin an image digest when you need a reproducible environment. Sandboxes created with version 3 or later of the JavaScript Sandbox SDK use vercel/sandbox/universal:latest by default. title: AWS PrivateLink endpoints are now available on Secure Compute
raw_summary: Enterprise teams using Secure Compute can now create and manage AWS PrivateLink endpoints directly from the Vercel dashboard. Endpoints on Secure Compute live in your team's dedicated VPC and use the network's AWS region. They belong to the network and are shared by its connected project environments. Vercel Functions , Vercel Sandbox , and builds connected to the network can reach AWS-hosted backends over the AWS private network. Before you add an endpoint in Vercel, the backend must already be exposed through a published AWS PrivateLink endpoint service. Examples include RDS, Aurora, Redshift, Snowflake, MongoDB Atlas, and internal services behind a Network Load Balancer. In Team Settings → Networking , open your Secure Compute network and choose Add Endpoint from the PrivateLink tab. Standard pricing for new endpoints: Each Secure Compute network includes one AWS PrivateLink endpoint. Additional endpoints cost $30 per month each. PrivateLink data transfer costs $0.04 per GB. Read the Secure Compute PrivateLink documentation to get started. Read more

title: Flags SDK now works on Vercel without FLAGS_SECRET
raw_summary: With flags@4.5.0 , projects on Vercel can use Flags Explorer and precompute without FLAGS_SECRET . That cuts out a setup step for new projects and removes the need to keep a shared secret in sync across microfrontends. Vercel signs Flags Explorer discovery requests and overrides, and the SDK encrypts flag values shown in the Vercel Toolbar with Vercel’s public key. Existing projects keep using FLAGS_SECRET while the environment variable is set or the secret is passed in code. Upgrading alone doesn't switch them to Vercel-managed keys. To use Vercel-managed keys for these features, remove the environment variable and any code that passes the secret explicitly. For local development, run vercel env pull . Precomputed codes created without a secret work only in the deployment that created them. Precompute without a secret requires Vercel system environment variables, which are enabled by default. Prebuilt deployments and codes that must work across deployments still need a secret; use FLAGS_PRECOMPUTE_SECRET if only precompute needs one. If you use a build cache, see the precompute documentation for the required configuration. Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation . Read more

title: Agents can now manage AI Gateway through Vercel MCP
raw_summary: Your agent can now manage AI Gateway through Vercel MCP . Ask it in plain language to: Manage virtual models : Create reusable model IDs with saved settings, then list, inspect, update, or restore them. Configure routing rules : View, add, and update team-wide rules that redirect requests to another model or block them.
