To create a virtual model, for example, ask your agent: Create a virtual model named coding-agent that uses anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 with Zero Data Retention enabled. Your apps and coding agents using AI Gateway can then use vmc/coding-agent as the model ID. You can change its model or settings later without updating those clients or redeploying your app. To get started, connect your agent to Vercel MCP with team-level access and the required AI Gateway permissions. Your Vercel team permissions still apply. Read more

title: Delete a run's data on demand in Workflow SDK
raw_summary: The Workflow SDK now lets you delete a finished run's stored data on demand. This feature gives you the ability to quickly meet compliance and security requirements when sensitive data needs to be purged from run payloads. Deleting a run's data deletes any inputs, outputs, hook payloads, and error traces for the run and its related entities. This does not delete the run's metadata : the run is still listed in observability. Attributes, hook tokens, and timings for steps and events can still be inspected. You can delete a run's data from the Vercel Dashboard, or via the CLI: You can also delete a run's data programmatically from your code: Deletion applies to finished runs only, so a run that is still going is skipped and keeps running. If you want to delete a run's payload as soon as it finishes, use the retention settings instead. Upgrade to workflow@5.7.0 or higher to use this feature. Learn more in the deleteRuns() reference . Read more

title: Inkling 2 Mini now available on AI Gateway
raw_summary: Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines is now available on AI Gateway. The small multimodal reasoning model is built for agentic coding, tool use, and knowledge work, with text and image inputs and text output. Inkling 2 Mini has 26.4 billion total parameters and 3.4 billion active per token. The model runs its middle layers more than once for every token, which lets it reason further before writing anything down and often reach an answer with fewer reasoning tokens. Like Inkling 2 Small, it is strongest on long-running agentic tasks. The model has a 1M-token context window, and reasoning effort can be set from none through max . Use thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini as the model name: To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Then select thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details. Try Inkling 2 Mini in the model playground . AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting , Zero Data Retention support , budgets for API keys , routing rules , and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. You can view all language models available on AI Gateway. Read more

title: AI Gateway now runs canary ZDR audits
raw_summary: AI Gateway now runs canary audits against inference providers to detect when prompt content is read outside the inference path. Contractual Zero Data Retention (ZDR) agreements and point-in-time security audits establish how a provider should handle your data, but production infrastructure changes continuously. Canary audits add a detection layer on top. Each canary audit run: Mints unique URLs that exist nowhere else, each mapped privately to a specific provider, model, and audit run. Sends prompts containing those URLs through the normal inference path, with ZDR requested for covered providers and non-ZDR pairs included as positive controls. Watches for traffic. A ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, so a canary URL should never receive a request. Records any request to a canary URL, identifying the provider, model, and run for investigation. Canary audits complement contractual ZDR agreements and independent audits rather than replacing them. Read more about AI Gateway security and compliance measures in the documentation . Read more

title: Kazunari Hanao joins Vercel as Country Manager, Japan
raw_summary: 日本語版はこちら： Vercel日本法人の代表に花尾和成が就任いたしました Kazunari Hanao has joined Vercel as Country Manager for Japan, based in Tokyo. His appointment is part of our continued investment in the Japanese market, including plans to expand our local team. Japanese developers were early adopters of Next.js. And today, Vercel's customers in Japan include Mitsubishi Corporation, Fujitsu Limited, U-NEXT CO., Ltd., and DeNA Co., Ltd., alongside startups like SANU Inc. and Reiwa Travel, Inc. Kazunari has spent the last decade building and leading software businesses in Japan. He joins Vercel from Pendo, where he was President of Pendo Japan. Before that, he built HashiCorp’s Japan business and spent nearly five years in sales leadership at Pivotal in Tokyo. I asked him about the opportunity in Japan and his decision to join Vercel. Why are you optimistic about Vercel's future in Japan? Japan is at a turning point in how software gets built. The country has innovative companies and talented developers, but complex enterprise IT environments are slowing the adoption of frontier AI to the point that businesses can’t capture its value. Vercel’s opportunity is to help Japanese enterprises move from experimentation to production, and run AI applications securely, reliably, and efficiently at scale. Cost, governance, and security for AI have become business priorities, not just technical ones. Almost every CXO I've met recently is working through those questions. What interested you in working for Vercel? I've always been drawn to technology that simplifies complexity and helps businesses move faster. Vercel felt like a natural continuation of that, with bigger potential. AI is transforming the whole software development lifecycle, and Vercel has a real chance to become a foundational platform for the next generation of applications. Ultimately what convinced me was the vision, the developer-first culture, and the chance to build something in Japan from the ground up. I enjoy building businesses, bringing talented people together, and creating an environment where teams feel empowered to take on hard problems. Vercel gives me the chance to do that with technology I believe in. What have you learned building businesses in Japan for global companies? Building a successful business is about much more than growing revenue. It starts with bringing together the right people, uniting them around a shared goal, earning the trust of customers and partners, and building a culture where every team member feels ownership. I've also learned how much it matters to connect global innovation with the specific needs of Japanese customers. During our first meetings, Guillermo and I talked about a future where countless digital services in Japan run on Vercel, and people experience its value every day whether they realize it or not. "Vercel Everywhere" is the future I want to build. What’s next in 2027 We're bringing our flagship conference, Ship, to Tokyo for the first time in 2027. It's a chance to hear directly from the Vercel team and from Japanese companies building on the platform. We'll share more details at vercel.com/ship in the new year. We’re also growing our Tokyo team across sales, solutions engineering, and partnerships. A larger local team will help us support Japanese customers and deepen our partnerships with Classmethod, AWS Japan, and Sitecore Japan. Watch our careers page for upcoming opportunities in Japan. title: Vercel日本法人の代表に花尾和成が就任いたしました
raw_summary: （本記事は、 英語版の就任発表 の日本語訳に、花尾本人の就任のご挨拶を加えたものです。） Vercel日本法人の代表に、 花尾和成 が就任いたしました（東京拠点）。今後、Vercelは花尾とともに国内のチームを拡充し、日本市場への投資をさらに進めていきます。 弊社が10年以上前に公開したNext.jsを、日本の開発者の皆さまはいち早く使い始めてくださいました。そして現在、日本では三菱商事、富士通、U-NEXT、ディー・エヌ・エーといった大企業から、SANUや令和トラベルといったスタートアップまで、幅広い企業にVercelをご利用いただいています。 花尾はこの10年間、日本でソフトウェア企業の運営にリーダーシップを発揮してきました。前職ではPendoの日本法人社長を務め、それ以前にはHashiCorpの日本事業を立ち上げ、Pivotalの東京オフィスで営業部門を統括しました。 就任にあたり、花尾から皆さまへのメッセージをご紹介します。 このたび、Vercelの日本法人代表に就任いたしました花尾和成です。私は20年以上IT業界に身を置き、そのうち10年以上は、開発者が開発そのものに集中できるようにするプロダクトに携わってまいりました。この経験を活かし、日本の開発者の皆さまと、その先にあるビジネスの価値を最大化することに貢献してまいります。 Vercelには、CEOのギシェルモ・ラウチを筆頭に、日本を好きなメンバーが数多くいます。こうした仲間の後押しを受けながら素晴らしいチームをつくり、Vercelが日本市場にとってかけがえのない存在となることを目指します。そして究極的には、直接的にも間接的にも、Vercelが日本のあらゆる場所で使われている世界を実現したいと考えています。 今後ともご指導ご鞭撻のほど、よろしくお願い申し上げます。 ここからは、私（Nick Bogaty, CRO）が聞き手を務めた花尾へのインタビューをお届けします。日本市場にどのような可能性を感じているのか、Vercelへの入社を決めた理由とあわせて伺いました。 Vercelが日本でさらに成長できるとお考えなのは、なぜですか？ 日本のソフトウェア開発は、まさに転換期を迎えています。日本には革新的な企業が多く、高い技術力を持つ開発者の皆さまが活躍されています。一方で、多くの企業では既存のシステムが複雑になり、最先端のAIの導入がなかなか進んでいません。その結果、AIを十分に活用できていないケースもあります。 日本企業がAIのポテンシャルを引き出すには、AIを試す段階から本番運用へ進む必要があります。Vercelは、その一歩を後押しできると考えています。AIアプリケーションを大規模に、安全かつ安定して、効率よく運用できるよう支える。これはまさに、Vercelが強みを発揮できる領域です。 そして、AIにかかるコストをどう管理するか、どんなルールで運用するか、セキュリティをどう確保するか。いまやどれも技術部門だけでなく、経営陣にとっても優先課題です。最近お会いした経営幹部の方々も、こうした課題に取り組んでいると口をそろえておっしゃっていました。この点でも、Vercelは日本企業の力になれると考えています。 Vercelへの入社を決めた理由をお聞かせください。 title: Introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway
raw_summary: AI is now used in every part of a business, and as a result, companies send source code, customer records, and regulated data through inference providers. The assurance that no data is retained after processing is still publicly unverified. Payment platforms, cloud infrastructure, and most other layers that handle data this sensitive have a way to prove their controls to outside parties, and inference will follow the same path. Today we are introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway. A provider is labeled Audited ZDR only after an independent security firm tests its zero data retention claims against its code, infrastructure, and live traffic, then publishes the report. Baseten , Modal , and Wafer are launch partners that have already begun audits, and more providers are encouraged to join to help raise the bar for security and privacy. Audited ZDR builds on two steps we took toward stronger governance earlier this year: We launched team-wide Zero Data Retention (ZDR) so teams could route traffic exclusively to providers stating a ZDR policy. We completed our ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification , which put Vercel’s own AI systems under independent third-party audit. We are now asking inference providers for the same thing we asked of ourselves: independent verification. Why a contract is not enough ZDR guarantees rely on contracts and self-attestation. A provider agrees not to retain prompts or completions, and customers take that commitment on faith. For teams sending proprietary code, customer information, or regulated data through models, self-reported ZDR contracts don't provide enough assurance. Are prompts landing in debug logs, crash dumps, or tracing pipelines? Can a rate limit push a request marked ZDR to a non-ZDR endpoint? Can a support engineer's debugging tools surface a customer's prompt? Answering these questions means running a bespoke security review for every provider and the models they host. An audit answers them in public. What Audited ZDR verifies To qualify for Audited ZDR on AI Gateway, an inference provider engages an independent security firm, chosen from among respected third-party auditors, to run the audit. The firm then tests the provider's zero data retention policy across the serving path for every model, endpoint, feature, and tool that handles AI Gateway traffic. The audit confirms that customer data is never written or retained on durable storage in any system. Customer data means prompts, completions, system prompts, embeddings, files, images and audio, tool and function-call payloads, and any derived data that could identify them. Coverage spans request logs, traces, metrics, crash dumps, prompt caches, abuse monitoring, analytics, backups, support tools, and training, fine-tuning, and evaluation datasets. The audit confirms that once a response is returned to AI Gateway, that content is deleted from the inference provider’s systems. Where a request uses caching, such as a KV cache, the cache stays in RAM only, is never written to disk, and the behavior is disclosed. The audit also confirms: That a request marked ZDR never fails over to a non-ZDR endpoint, tool, or feature That no human or automated process accesses customer data outside handling the request itself That sub-processors with access comply with all of the above That no training on customer data occurs Auditors verify this by reviewing the inference provider's serving-path source code and infrastructure configuration, then running live tests. They send marked prompts through AI Gateway and search the provider's logging, caching, and storage systems for any trace of them. Every passing provider publishes the report under the auditor's name. It covers scope, methodology, dates, findings, and fix status, with any exceptions disclosed and redactions limited to exploit detail. AI Gateway links directly to the report. Canary monitoring between audits An independent audit checks a provider's code and infrastructure at a point in time, but production systems change. To add a detection layer between independent audits, Vercel also runs canary audits against inference providers on AI Gateway. Each run sends prompts containing unique, unindexed URLs mapped privately to a provider, model, and run. Because a ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, any request to a canary URL triggers an investigation into the provider and model involved. Canary checks cannot detect prompts written to disk and never read, so they complement independent code and infrastructure audits rather than replacing them. How Audited ZDR works in AI Gateway We are adding an independently Audited ZDR provider tier and a team-wide toggle in AI Gateway policy settings. When enabled, AI Gateway routes and fails over your team's requests only across providers with published audits that meet the bar. Launch partners have started their audits, and each provider enters the tier as soon as its report is published. Launch partner reports are expected to be published by December 8, 2026. About AI Gateway AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries and failover for higher uptime than connecting to providers directly. It reflects provider pricing with no markup and charges no platform fee on inference, including Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. Read the AI Gateway documentation to get started. The audited tier works alongside AI Gateway's other compliance controls. Regional inference pins where a provider runs inference to the US, EU, Australia, or Japan, per request or team-wide, and any data the provider stores at rest stays in that region. If AI Gateway can't honor the region, the request fails rather than running elsewhere. Provider headquarters filters routing by who owns the provider, so a request only reaches providers whose parent company is headquartered in a country you allow. Private inference connects your own self-hosted or fine-tuned model endpoints to AI Gateway, called as private/<slug> with the same SDKs, auth, and observability as catalog models and scoped to your team. Read more

title: AI Gateway now supports extraction models
raw_summary: Extraction models are now on AI Gateway. They find specific details in the content you provide, such as an invoice number or contact names, and return them as separate fields your code can use. ScaleDown Extract-1 is the first available extraction model. It extracts text values or lists of text values from text, images, and PDFs. You can use it to process invoices, contracts, and other records. Extraction is currently available through the AI SDK only. With ai@7.0.176 or later, use experimental_extract and the model ID scaledown/extract-1 : Each key in fields has an entry in result.answers . If a field is not found, its value is null . Extract-1 returns confidence scores from 0 to 1 for matches, including individual list items, so you can flag uncertain results for review. For text input, it can also return character offsets showing where a match appears. To extract from a PDF or image, pass it as a file part in state : Extraction requests appear in AI Gateway logs and spend tracking. See the extraction quickstart for setup and authentication. title: Catch missing feature flags before they reach production
raw_summary: Vercel Flags can now block a deployment from reaching production if you’ve declared a flag in code but haven’t created it in your project. Without that definition, your app can silently fall back to the flag’s default value, even if that turns on a feature you meant to keep off. The Flag Definitions Present Deployment Check runs when a deployment is ready. If any flags are missing, the check fails and lists them in the results, where you can create each one before redeploying. The check reads your Flags SDK discovery endpoint. With flags@4.5.0 or later on Vercel, it works without FLAGS_SECRET ; earlier versions still require the secret. To turn on blocking, teams on all plans can enable the check in their project’s Build and Deployment settings and mark it as required. See the Deployment Checks documentation for setup details. Read more

title: Choose AI Gateway providers by headquarters country
raw_summary: Provider headquarters sends your AI Gateway requests only to providers headquartered in countries you choose, so you can meet compliance and procurement rules about where your AI vendors are located. You can configure provider headquarters to be an allowlist of the countries to use, or a denylist of the countries to block. AI Gateway skips providers in blocked countries and routes requests to the rest of the list, so a model stays accessible as long as it is available in one of its allowed provider locations. Use provider headquarters with regional hosting and regional inference to control where a request is received, where the model runs, and who runs it. Set provider headquarters for your team Pro and Enterprise customers can apply their provider headquarters list to every AI Gateway request across their team. Configure the list in AI Gateway settings . Provider headquarters settings are applied automatically as AI Gateway adds models and providers. Providers without a headquarters country on record never receive your requests. Set provider headquarters per request On any plan, set headquarters in the gateway provider options to restrict a single request. Pass country codes for an allowlist, or prefix every code with ! for a denylist, as in ['!US'] . If your team has a list, a request can only narrow it. In the examples below, requests are only sent to providers based in the US and Germany: Both settings filter providers, so a model stays available as long as one of its providers is based in an allowed country. If no provider is available in an allowed country, AI Gateway tries your fallback models. If no fallback models are available in allowed countries, or if no fallback models are configured, the request will fail without trying to route to providers in other locations. Read the provider headquarters documentation for the countries supported, pricing and setup details. Read more

title: Vercel Functions now support request bodies up to 20MiB
raw_summary: Vercel Functions now accept inbound request bodies up to 20MiB, up from 4.5MB, in Public Beta. To turn this on, set the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1 environment variable. The opt-in applies to the whole project in the environment where you set it, so you can test the larger limit on preview before enabling it in production. It requires the project's functions to use the performance memory setting of 4GB. It applies to functions on the Node.js, Python, and Bun runtimes, and to Routing Middleware. Functions and Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime keep the 4.5MB cap and return 413 on oversize bodies, so moving them onto the larger limit means switching to the Node.js runtime with runtime: 'nodejs' , or proxy.ts in Next.js. When a project opts in, Routing Middleware receives request headers and metadata but no request body, enforced at the project level. Middleware still runs and still sees every other request header, so body-dependent middleware behavior is the one thing that becomes unavailable. This avoids sending the body twice, to both middleware and the target function, which would raise cost and time to first byte. When handling larger request bodies, read the body promptly and avoid holding it in memory to prevent backpressure and memory issues. Learn more in the Vercel Functions limitations documentation . title: Vercel completes ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification
raw_summary: Vercel has completed its ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, meeting the international standard for AI management systems. This certification gives our customers confidence to ship fast with agents on Vercel, demonstrating how Vercel designs, builds, operates, and governs our AI products. Our AI management system covers Vercel’s underlying infrastructure and core AI products, including AI Gateway, Vercel Agent, v0, AI-based open source software and frameworks, as well as the people and processes behind them. Vercel’s certificate is available here , and additional audit documentation is available through our Trust Center . What is ISO 42001? ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard for AI management systems and applies to any organization that develops, provides, or uses AI. An AI management system is the set of policies, roles, processes, and controls through which an organization consistently governs AI activities. The standard includes requirements for leadership accountability, AI risk assessment, lifecycle management, data governance, transparency, and continual improvement. The requirement that makes ISO 42001 distinct from security standards is the AI system impact assessment. Security frameworks cover how an organization protects information, but ISO 42001 covers how it builds and uses AI, including the assessment of how an AI system impacts the people it touches, and the benefits and harms that would result when that system materially changes. To obtain the certification, we underwent a two-stage audit performed by an independent, accredited certification body, which evaluated whether our AI management system is designed correctly and operates effectively. The certificate is valid for three years, with annual surveillance audits in between. “Enterprises want agents in production, but no one should have to choose between moving fast with AI and governing it well,” said Talha Tariq, CTO for Security. “We built our AI governance to run as continuously as we ship, and ISO 42001 is the independent check that it works.” What this means for customers AI moved into the critical path of how software gets built faster than the governance around it did. Teams are shipping agents, assistants, and model-backed features on Vercel every day, and the questions that follow are no longer hypothetical: Who is accountable when a model behaves unexpectedly? What data reached a model? How is the system monitored once it’s live? Who decided the system was ready? We pursued ISO 42001 because we are committed to providing enterprise-grade AI products. This certification attests that we run deliberate, auditable AI systems. How we govern AI at Vercel There are three primary ways AI is governed at Vercel. Impact assessments Vercel conducts AI system impact assessments which cover foreseeable benefits, harms, failures, and misuse. We reassess these risks and benefits when the system materially changes. Evaluations before release We maintain evals for our AI systems covering performance, safety, and security, with human review for material changes. Clear data commitments Where it is not the default option based on pricing plan, we provide customers the ability to set their data handling preferences ranging from zero data retention (ZDR) to training opt-out. Our AI policy is available at v0.app/policy. Ship fast, with confidence We are committed to helping teams ship fast with confidence in the way AI is built and governed at Vercel. ISO 42001 is proof of that commitment, giving our customers: Confidence in agentic infrastructure: Vercel’s AI systems have been audited, which means customers using our AI products start from a reviewed foundation instead of an unexamined one. Governance can ship at the speed of the product: Agents now drive the development and deployment of applications. Governance and oversight that occurs quarterly can’t govern software that changes hourly, so we built a system that reviews AI as continuously as we ship it. Simplified and accelerated assurance: Customers and partners can rely on this certification, alongside our other compliance attestations, to meet AI governance diligence requirements for faster third-party vendor onboarding. Clear lines of responsibility: ISO 42001 requires that responsibilities be allocated across the AI supply chain. Our documentation outlines what Vercel is accountable for and what remains yours, the same shared-responsibility model we use for security. Discipline that holds over time: Annual surveillance audits mean this isn’t a one-time claim. As our AI products change, the system that governs them stays under independent review. AI is changing what people build on Vercel, and we intend for the governance around it to keep pace. We’ll continue to expand the scope of our certifications as our products grow. Read more

title: Agents can now find Vercel CLI commands by describing the task
raw_summary: Coding agents can now use vercel help search to find Vercel CLI commands by describing a task in plain language. The search returns a list of matching commands. Add --with-help to include the help page for the first result in the same call. For example, vercel help search "roll back production" --with-help returns the options and examples for vercel rollback . Search also supports: API endpoints: When a Vercel API endpoint matches the task, search returns a vercel api command with the request path and placeholders for every required input. The agent can fill in the values without guessing the path. JSON output: Use --json to return search results as JSON. Combine it with --with-help to include usage instructions, options, and examples for the first result. Search recognizes common wording, such as “show” instead of “list,” and handles minor spelling mistakes. The CLI also includes a skill that tells coding agents to start with vercel help search when looking for a command. Vercel doesn't log your search text. Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade . Read more

title: Priority Projects now in public beta
raw_summary: Priority Projects are now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. This optional upgrade for individual Vercel projects adds bot and traffic-source signals, Page Integrity for monitoring and controlling client-side scripts and connections, and additional Firewall controls and alerts. Bot signals Bot protection is free on all plans. You can enable it to challenge non-browser traffic while allowing verified bots. Priority adds more detailed bot signals: categories, verification status, and names where available. Use these signals in: Firewall rules: Match on bot_name , bot_category , bot_status , and bot_protection in the dashboard or with vercel firewall rules add . Application code: Read x-vercel-bot-category , x-vercel-bot-name , and x-vercel-verified-bot from request headers in Routing Middleware and Vercel Functions. See the header reference for verified and claimed bot names. Logs and Observability: Logs show the Firewall action on all plans. Priority adds the matched rule and bot details where available. In Firewall Observability, Priority adds botCategory for unverified traffic. Log Drains also include bot classifications. Traffic Sources Priority adds Traffic Sources labels for requests from Tor exit nodes, VPNs, open or anonymizing proxies, and residential proxies. It also labels traffic flagged by abuse blocklists. Use these labels in custom Firewall rules, analyze them in Firewall Observability, or read them from the x-vercel-waf-source request header in your application. A request can have multiple labels. Use the Traffic Sources managed ruleset to log, challenge, or block traffic by source category. Review matching traffic before enabling blocking, since these categories can also include legitimate users. To enable the Traffic Sources managed ruleset from the CLI, run vercel firewall managed-rulesets enable traffic-sources . This stages the change; review it with vercel firewall diff , then apply it with vercel firewall publish . Page Integrity Priority Projects get access to Page Integrity to monitor client-side scripts and connections, receive alerts when new scripts or connections are detected, and block unapproved resources. Page Integrity maintains a resource inventory and uses Content Security Policy (CSP) for discovery and enforcement, without adding client-side JavaScript. It operates in three stages: Detect: Discover scripts using report-only CSP headers on sampled requests. Review: Approve or reject scripts and record business justifications. Block: Enforce a CSP that blocks scripts outside the approved inventory. Page Integrity must be enabled separately. Configure monitoring and review resources in the dashboard; the CLI can also show its resource inventory: Firewall controls and alerts Anomaly alerts DDoS alerts are available on all plans. Priority adds anomaly alerts for bot traffic and requests matching system or custom Firewall rules. Use these alerts to investigate potential attacks and unusual traffic patterns. Configure notifications in your team’s Settings > Alerts , with delivery options including email, Slack, and webhooks. View recent alerts with vercel alerts --since 24h . To manage alert configuration from the CLI, see vercel monitors . OWASP Core Ruleset On Pro, Priority lets you enable the OWASP Core Ruleset to protect against common web application attacks. Enterprise projects can already enable it without Priority. Add it as a team default from Security > Rules , or enable it for a linked project via the CLI with vercel firewall managed-rulesets enable owasp --yes followed by vercel firewall publish . OWASP inspection is billed separately per inspected request and GB of inspected payload. Response-based rate limiting Priority adds response conditions to the rate-limit rules available on all plans. Count requests toward a limit only when their responses match specified HTTP status codes or response headers. For example, count 401 responses from failed login attempts or 404 responses for missing pages, rather than every matching request. Higher Firewall limits Priority increases the following per-project limits (shown as standard → with Priority): Get started Priority costs $200 per project per month. Enable it from your project’s Firewall or Settings page, or with the CLI. For the CLI, update to the latest version with vercel upgrade , then enable Priority for the project you want to upgrade: Page Integrity usage is billed separately. Its standard rate is $2 per 1,000 monitored page views, with each view covering up to 100 scripts. Learn more in the Priority Projects documentation . Read more

title: When the unthinkable happens: perceptions of monetary policy in tail events
raw_summary: Focus Public perceptions of monetary policy play a central role in determining the effectiveness of policy actions. Despite central banks’ efforts to improve communication, the public has an incomplete understanding of how policymakers respond to economic shocks. This challenge becomes particularly acute during rare and severe shocks, or “tail events”, that fall outside past experience. In such circumstances, misperceptions about monetary policy can amplify economic fluctuations and undermine stabilisation efforts. In this paper we examine how public perceptions of monetary policy evolve following tail events and whether misperceptions can amplify and propagate their macroeconomic effects. Contribution We develop a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model in which private agents – households and firms – have incomplete information about both the central bank’s response to inflation and the distribution of economic shocks. They simultaneously learn about monetary policy and the nature of shocks by observing economic outcomes. We examine how this learning process shapes inflation and output dynamics following large adverse oil supply shocks. We also test the relevance of this process using US data, estimating a nonlinear vector autoregression model with exogenous variables in which the effects of oil supply shocks depend on their size. This enables us to compare how small and large shocks affect views about monetary policy responsiveness, inflation expectations and macroeconomic outcomes. Findings We find that large adverse supply shocks lead private agents to underestimate how strongly the central bank responds to inflation. Because such shocks are rare, agents initially underestimate their likelihood and interpret part of the resulting inflation increase as evidence of a weaker monetary policy response. These misperceptions raise inflation expectations, generating persistent inflation and a temporary increase in output above its usual level. This is especially the case following large shocks, while small shocks have limited effects on agents’ beliefs. Evidence from US data supports these findings, showing that large oil supply shocks are associated with lower perceptions of monetary policy responsiveness, persistent inflation expectations and output overshooting. Our findings highlight the importance of central bank communication and credibility in stabilising expectations during tail events. ______________________________________________________________________ For webstaging purposes, please add: Abstract We study how public perceptions of monetary policy evolve when the economy experiences rare and severe supply shocks. When agents learn in real time about the distribution of the shocks and the monetary policy reaction function, they tend to underestimate the strength of the response to inflation following large but infrequent negative supply shocks. Embedding this mechanism in a general equilibrium model with learning, we show that it endogenously generates inflation dynamics persistently above target and temporary output overshooting after a tail event. Using U.S. data, we find empirical evidence supporting our model's predictions about the distinctive role of tail events in shaping policy perceptions and macroeconomic dynamics. Our findings indicate that public misperceptions can amplify and prolong the aggregate effects of tail events, potentially undermining central banks' stabilization efforts.

title: Immigrants' skills and capital deepening: evidence from Chile
raw_summary: We study the effect of migration on firms’ capital deepening, leveraging a massive influx of immigrant workers with varying skill sets from Venezuela and Haiti in Chile between 2015 and 2019.

title: "Eppur si muove": convergence within and between countries
raw_summary: Kremer, Willis, and You (2022) report that over six decades richer countries lost their growth advantage. Acemoglu and Molina (2022) and Pesaran and Smith (2026) reply that such regressions cannot measure catch-up when countries head toward different moving destinations.

title: The gig economy and digital payments
raw_summary: The growth of the “gig” economy could have far-reaching implications for payment systems. Gig work involves digital platforms that intermediate between workers and (retail or business) customers, in areas as diverse as ride-hailing and food delivery, freelance design and professional services, and customer service.

title: Ready-to-run global liquidity stress tests for banks and banking systems
raw_summary: Liquidity risk remains a persistent threat to financial stability, as starkly demonstrated by the 2023 banking turmoil in the United States and Europe. Hence, the ability to quickly gauge banks’ liquidity risks could prove useful especially during periods of market stress, but also to assess differences in liquidity buffers across peer economies and banks.

title: US monetary policy, macroeconomic news and the global secular decline of interest rates
raw_summary: The global secular decline in long-term interest rates since the 1990s has been largely driven by cumulative yield changes during U.S. monetary policy announcement windows (FOMC windows).

title: Hedge portfolio optimisation with Sinkhorn-type algorithms
raw_summary: Algorithms are proposed to construct efficient hedge portfolios with complex greeks

title: Refined slippage: variance reduction using counterfactual returns
raw_summary: A new metric is introduced that benchmarks fill prices against counterfactual prices, rather than the arrival price

title: Numerai Monthly: Unity Dataset & Tooling, Tournament Unification, Community Updates
raw_summary: Introducing the Unity Dataset Numerai released Unity, a new dataset with 1,040 features and real stock identifiers. Users can now source external data and engineer their own features, enabling AI agents to participate in more of the quantitative research process. Unity is currently available for both Numerai and Numerai

title: As Corporate Bond Markets Grow, Is Bank Lending Shrinking?
raw_summary: The size of global corporate bond markets has increased dramatically over the past three decades. As of the end of 2024, nonfinancial corporate bonds issued by U.S. firms accounted for 29 percent of U.S. GDP. In other advanced economies, though bond markets remain smaller than in the U.S., corporate bonds were on average 11 percent of GDP in the same year. This growth is usually read as a shift from bank to market finance. But the ratio of bonds to GDP can rise either because firms take more debt in general, or because firms shift the composition of their debt toward bonds. In this post, we document growth in bonds to GDP for both the U.S. and other advanced economies, and argue that the sources of that growth are different across countries and have changed over time.

title: What Do Foreign Trends Tell Us About Future U.S. Labor Force Dynamics?
raw_summary: Growth in the U.S. working-age population has fallen to near zero with the recent sharp drop in net immigration. Given the ongoing decline in the native-born working-age population, the available labor supply could soon begin to shrink. The demographic path the U.S. may soon navigate has already been trod by several other advanced economies that have experienced more rapid population aging and historically lower immigration. This post lays out the basic facts about advanced economy (AE) experiences since 2014 and raises the prospect that the demographic headwinds long visible abroad may now be coming into clear view at home.

title: Does the Stock Market Stigmatize Banks that Borrow from the Fed?
raw_summary: Banks may resist borrowing from the Federal Reserve during a panic if such borrowing is stigmatized (that is, viewed by the market as a sign of financial weakness), thus hampering the Fed’s ability to resolve the crisis. The problem may be particularly acute for publicly traded banks since their stock prices immediately reflect the market's opinion of them. In this post, based on a recent paper , we track what happened to stock investors' perceptions of a bank's risk level right after it first borrowed from Fed facilities in the first month of the bank run of 2023 . We find that, after a first trip to the Fed's Discount Window (DW), investors became more sensitive to that bank's weaknesses. In contrast, investors did not evince such concern when the bank took a first loan from a new facility, the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP).

title: Can Workers Predict Job Finding and Job Loss?
raw_summary: Workers’ perceptions of the labor market may differ from aggregate labor market statistics. Individuals might be overly optimistic about their chance of finding a job, or too pessimistic about the odds of losing their current position. In this post, we compare subjective beliefs of future job-finding and job-loss from the New York Fed’s Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE) with their realized counterparts in the Current Population Survey (CPS). We then investigate how closely aggregate perceptions of job-finding and job-loss prospects align with realized rates.

title: Banking System Vulnerability: 2026 Update
raw_summary: As in previous years, we provide in this post an update on the vulnerability of the U.S. banking system based on four analytical models that capture different aspects of this vulnerability. We use data through 2026:Q2 to update our analysis and discuss how the vulnerability measures have changed since our last update one year ago .

title: A Look at the Wider Divide in Credit Card Delinquency by Income
raw_summary: Credit card delinquency rose sharply between 2022 and 2024, and the increase was steepest among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods. Here, we check in on credit card performance by neighborhood income and trace when the borrowers who are now struggling with their payments were issued cards. We find that during the pandemic, an increasing share of new credit cards went to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress.

title: Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150‑Year Perspective
raw_summary: Has U.S. monetary policy actually improved over time? Or was the apparent success of the modern Federal Reserve mostly the result of more favorable economic conditions and better luck? In this post, we summarize our paper , * which develops a framework for comparing monetary policy across different economic environments. Our approach asks how close policy came to the best response given the economic conditions and shocks policymakers faced. Applying this framework to 150 years of U.S. monetary history, we find that meaningful improvements in monetary policy occurred only in the last thirty years. Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.

title: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence
raw_summary: Benjamin Guin Most discussion of AI in organisations focuses on productivity: as analysis becomes cheaper, decision-making should improve. This post argues that an important consequence lies elsewhere. Where the relevant information is accessible, a wider range of people can produce professionally presented analysis and submit it to decision-makers. Responsibility for decisions, however, remains concentrated and … Continue reading AI, accountability and the economics of evidence →

title: FEDS Paper: Collateral Mobility and the Lender of Last Resort
raw_summary: Antonis Kotidis Using confidential Federal Reserve Discount Window data from March 2023, I study collateral mobility in lender-of-last-resort lending. Banks with prior experience were more likely to post loan collateral and did so two days faster than inexperienced peers, while showing little effect for securities collateral. When loan collateral was pledged to FHLBs, redeployment to the Fed slowed by an additional three to four days, even among sophisticated banks, because of absent subordination agreements and different collateral reporting practices. In fast runs, what matters is not only where collateral sleeps, but how fast it can move when it needs to wake up.

title: FEDS Paper: The Welfare Effects of Bank Liquidity and Capital Requirements(Revised)
raw_summary: Skander J. Van den Heuvel and Sergio Villalvazo The stringency of bank liquidity and capital requirements should depend on their social costs and benefits. Equilibrium asset returns yield two simple formulas that express the welfare cost of each requirement as a function of observable variables only. Based on U.S. data, the welfare cost of a 10% liquidity requirement is equivalent to a permanent loss in consumption of about 0.02%, a modest impact. Even using conservative measurements, the cost of a similarly sized increase in the capital requirement is roughly tenfold. Still, optimal policy relies on both requirements to mitigate moral hazard from deposit insurance and is close to Basel III levels.

title: FEDS Paper: Where's The Bank? Banking Access in the Era of Branch Consolidation(Revised)
raw_summary: Robert M. Adams and Shane M. Sherlund The number of U.S. bank branches fell more than 19 log points between 2014 and 2024, prompting concerns about eroding access to banking services. We study this contraction using a free-entry, two-dimensional spatial competition model in the tradition of Lösch and Hotelling. The model predicts that equilibrium branch density scales linearly with local customer density and that the elasticity of mean nearest-branch distance with respect to the number of branches is -1/2 . Using branch locations and census-block-level data on households and employment, we estimate elasticities between -0.37 and -0.52. These lie near the two-dimensional prediction and reject the -1 implied by one-dimensional models. Differences in branch access across demographic groups are economically small, and they did not widen over the decade. The branch contraction is consistent with the equilibrium response of a competitive spatial system to an industry-wide profitability shock, rather than a localized withdrawal of service.

title: FEDS Paper: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
raw_summary: Nick Carollo , Leland D. Crane , Daniel Garcia Molina , and Joseph Nichols We assess the current evidence on how AI-related investment and the use of AI are affecting the U.S. macroeconomy. Specifically, we document the boom in data center capital investment, the current rate of adoption of AI tools in the economy, the impact of the AI-related investment surge on prices, and discuss whether AI tools have affected the labor market and productivity yet. Driven by current and expected future demand for AI services, investment in data centers, both the physical structures and semiconductor chips and other IT equipment inside the structures, has climbed sharply. AI adoption is growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all. AI model-producing firms have also grown extremely fast, and now account for a noticeable fraction of software industry gross output. Prices have climbed in sectors that provide direct inputs to the data centers, such as memory chips. Effects on the labor market so far appear small and somewhat mixed. Similarly, the effects of AI on aggregate productivity growth also appear to be small so far, and the recent pickup in productivity likely reflects factors that predated the diffusion on generative AI.

title: FEDS Paper: Costly Misdemeanours: Labour Market Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving Violations
raw_summary: Kabir Dasgupta , Marco Francesconi, Jonathan James, Linda Kirkpatrick, and Alexander Plum This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market outcomes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after conviction to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.

title: Highlights from the 2026 CAIRFI AI Workshop
raw_summary: How Capital One and Columbia University are partnering to advance responsible AI and machine learning in financial technology. On Oct. 13, Capital One and Columbia University co-hosted the Capital One Center for AI and Responsible Financial Innovation (CAIRFI) Workshop. The event gathered researchers, scientists and academic leaders to share insights on artificial intelligence and machine learning. The workshop served as a key collaboration milestone. Its mission was to exchange research insights, build relationships ahead of the upcoming academic year 2026–2027 call for proposals and connect Capital One applied researchers with Columbia faculty and doctoral candidates. Through a series of lightning talks, panel discussions and a poster session, attendees explored critical areas of AI research. Columbia Engineering Dean Shih-Fu Chang delivered the opening remarks, setting the stage for three focused tracks: Fundamental Model Research, Agentic Systems and Applications & Humans. While the workshop featured presentations and discussions from across the partnership, three lightning talks provided a detailed look at the applied research happening within Capital One. Advancing fundamental model research The first session featured lightning talks from Micah Goldblum, Adam Block, James Anderson and Alfy Samuel. Samuel, senior director in AI foundations at Capital One, presented her research on uncertainty quantification, “Confidence-Based Response Abstinence: Improving LLM Trustworthiness via Activation-Based Uncertainty Estimation,” published at EMNLP 2025 . The work addresses the need for trustworthy large language models (LLMs) in high-stakes domains by teaching models to abstain from answering when they lack confidence. Instead of relying on token probabilities, the method uses raw feed-forward activations over answer tokens as a single-pass signal for a lightweight confidence probe. When deployed in a financial customer-support application, the confidence filter improved precision to 0.95 by withholding low-confidence answers instead of generating incorrect responses. The team is currently extending this uncertainty quantification work to multiagent systems. Evaluating agentic systems The second track focused on agentic systems, featuring presentations from Kathy McKeown, Zhou Yu, Simha Sethumadhavan and Genta Winata. Winata, director of applied research at Capital One, shared insights from the paper “T1-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Scenario Agents in Real-World Domains” published at EMNLP 2026 . Winata noted that existing agentic benchmarks primarily test models in isolated single-domain scenarios and lack the compositional complexity needed for real-world applications. To address this, T1-Bench offers a high-fidelity framework featuring interleaved scenarios and multiturn user-assistant interactions across 25 distinct domains and 76 executable tools. The research highlights the ongoing challenge of reliably orchestrating tools across complex multidomain environments, with Gemma 4–31B-IT achieving the highest overall pass rate during the evaluations. Modeling user events and applications The final session highlighted applications and human interaction with talks from Baishakhi Ray, Lydia Chilton and Rizal Fathony. Fathony, an applied researcher at Capital One, discussed methods for integrating sequential and relational modeling for user events. His presentation explored how to combine the fine-grained chronological tracking of sequential modeling with the broad interaction view of relational graph modeling. Fathony detailed an end-to-end framework called BRIDGE, which processes sequences into dynamic node features and optimizes parameters jointly across both modules to better predict user behavior. The model consistently outperformed both static and temporal graph baselines across multiple datasets. Expanding the research pipeline Following the sessions, Bayan Bruss, vice president of applied research at Capital One, opened an evening networking reception and poster session. Speaking to over 100 registered doctoral candidates, Bruss highlighted the CAIRFI center’s role as a hub for exploring the intersection of advanced research and financial technology. He also outlined opportunities for students to engage with massive datasets and scalable infrastructure through applied research, AI engineering and data science internships . By bridging academic research and real-world application, the workshop established a strong foundation for future proposals and the next generation of industry innovators. title: A modern dilemma: Consume data from a stream or a lake
raw_summary: Data is a critical component of software architecture, providing the foundation for business processes, including those powered by artificial intelligence (AI). Quality, volume, latency, consistency, ordering and duplicates are essential considerations in software design. Modern cloud architectures consume data in various ways, such as through application programming interfaces (APIs), streams and data lakes. You can consume data at the individual event or record level as it arrives or in larger batches. Legacy architectures often process data in scheduled batches, forcing surrounding architecture and business processes to depend on that approach. Getting the data consumption approach right up front is vital, because rearchitecting later is costly. General patterns to consume data There are several general data consumption patterns. These include APIs (record-by-record or multirecord results), event stream consumption (record-by-record), Delta Change Data Feed (CDF) consumption (record-by-record) or traditional batch ETL-extract, transform, load (multirecord results). APIs are ideal for low-latency, record-by-record requirements. They also support multirecord results, typically through pagination. APIs usually follow a synchronous approach, where the client makes a call and waits for a response before moving to the next step. Model Context Protocol is an industry specification for agents to consume data and can support record-by-record or batch results via pagination, similar to APIs. They are often a wrapper on top of APIs. The event stream pattern works well for sub-second latency requirements and typically runs on a tech stack like Kafka, Flink or Spark Streaming. These technologies excel at record-level calculations (like on-the-fly calculation), transformations (like column mapping) or enrichment (like adding data to an existing event). Delta Lake is often used in data lakes and serves as a transaction log to standard Apache Parquet data files ( source ). CDF is a Delta Lake feature that tracks row-level changes (inserts, updates and deletes) between table versions ( source) . Delta CDF consumption is an alternative for handling record-level calculations compared to the event stream pattern, with a few key differences. Latency can still be low but rarely sub-second. The tech stack consists only of a Spark job and an Amazon S3 bucket, simplifying complexity and maintenance. This pattern provides higher cost efficiency for high-volume data. At extreme volumes (2 million per second), streaming can delay, especially during event replay. Traditional batch ETL handles record groups and performs joins across many source datasets. Similar to Delta CDF, Spark and S3 can implement batch ETL. The key difference is the presence of many more source and destination datasets. These jobs run at massive scale with significant compute power. Consistency, ordering and duplicates Many considerations inform data consumption design. Consistency is one of the first to be defined: Does your design need strong or eventual consistency? Strong consistency means the process requires a response before proceeding to get the current state as of that exact moment and is often blocking or synchronous. Eventual consistency means processing will eventually get a response and is asynchronous (nonblocking). See the illustration below for details. Strong consistency vs. eventual consistency Ordering Order is another important consideration. Do you need to consume data in the exact order it was produced, or does order not matter? It is essential to understand which technology patterns preserve the original order of the data so consumers can take appropriate action. Kafka, for example, does not guarantee order across partitions when using multiple partitions. Kafka ordering within a single partition vs. across multiple partitions Duplicates At-least-once delivery and exactly-once delivery describe the nature of duplicates. At-least-once delivery guarantees data delivery at least once, meaning it could arrive multiple times and result in duplicates. Exactly-once delivery guarantees the message will be delivered only once. Kafka Streams supports exactly-once delivery. Consumers need these details to set proper expectations and design processes appropriately. With at-least-once delivery patterns, producers can use data keys that enable consumers to deduplicate data. With data lakes, one approach to eliminating duplicate records is an upsert mode that checks keys to see whether a record already exists. If it does, the system updates it; if not, it inserts it. At-least-once vs. exactly-once delivery comparison Use case characteristics of consumption patterns We categorize our five general patterns into two buckets: traditional batch ETL processing and real-time processing (e.g., APIs, event streams, Delta CDF). The use case characteristics below inform when data should be consumed via batch or a real-time pattern. Traditional batch ETL processing Batch ETL processing executes against a large batch set of data rather than individual records as they arrive. The following use case characteristics are a good fit: Processing requires more than a day’s worth of historical data. This data is used within transformation logic, enabling sophisticated calculations, trend analysis and the derivation of insightful features based on historical patterns and context. Doing this in a stream takes longer and may not scale, depending on data volume. Processing requires an entire day’s worth of data. These use cases require collecting an entire dataset before processing to ensure data quality, consistency and adherence to downstream formats. Joining large datasets spanning large time windows. This performs efficient, scalable joins across extensive datasets, using optimized algorithms and distributed computing frameworks to handle complex relationships without compromising performance. Real-time processing (e.g., APIs, event stream, Delta CDF) Real-time processing requires immediate data handling and transformation as it arrives, enabling timely insights and actions. The following use case characteristics are a good fit: Executing row-level transformations. This involves applying specific functions or logic to individual data records upon ingestion. Transformations can include data cleansing, standardization, enrichment or the creation of derived fields. This granular processing ensures data accuracy and prepares it for subsequent analysis or integration. Performing data transformations upon API calls. This allows dynamic data manipulation based on external information retrieved through API interactions. As real-time data arrives, the system makes a call to an external service to fetch additional context or perform specific processing steps. These API results further transform incoming data, enabling richer processing. Initiating real-time API calls based on incoming data streams. This feature enables the immediate application of logic or models when receiving incoming data streams. By invoking inference APIs in real time, organizations generate predictions, classifications or anomaly detections as events occur. This is vital for proactive decision-making, personalized experiences and automated responses. Executing real-time joins between a data stream and a static dataset. This join combines a continuously flowing stream of real-time data with a relatively unchanging dataset. This enriches streaming data with reference information, such as looking up customer details, product information or geographical location. The static nature of one dataset allows efficient, rapid lookups during real-time processing.
